SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION

Interview with John Collins
by Patricia Willard

Washington, D. C.
April 21, 1975

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.
PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE
AREA CODE 202 347-5395
P R O C E E D I N G S
MS. WILLARD: Interview with John Collins. April 21, 1975. Do you want to proceed chronologically, start with the beginning in Montgomery, Alabama, your earliest musical influences.

Yes. Well, my mother was a very good pianist, and my grandmother was a very good pianist, and they taught music, played. My mother was something else though. And she also worked at this particular time real early, and when I was very small she worked for W. C. Handy, as a demonstration pianist. She and Fletcher Henderson. So I was always exposed to just about the best there was in music.
Would you explain demonstration.

Well, as I understand it they would play new tunes and things. People would come into buy, say the music stores, and Fletcher and my mother would play the piano and, you know, demonstrate the tunes. Yeah.
I didn't realize W. C. Handy had had--
a music store
Yes. Evidently he did. You know, this is --
You don't remember.

I don't remember any of this. But I think in his book he's got something about my mother also. But any way, so consequently I was always exposed to just about the best in music, you know, from the classics just right on
down the line. It was a funny thing, they never wanted me to play piano. They never wanted me to play the piano. And I just --
Who didn't want you?
My mother didn't, nor my grandmother. They tried to discourage me from playing, and it's something I never understood.
Did they ever say why?

No, never said why. But despite that I just got into it, you know, and my mother recognized it very early, so she kind of took me under her wing, and she had bands and I always played with her bands, even when I was in well at that time short pants, you know.
When was that?

Well, that was from around 12, 13. I was playing, you know, with her band then. And she had let's see one guy I remember particularly, his name was Lorenzo Wardell. He had played with let's see -- was it McKinney's cotton pickers? From Detroit. Yeah, a very fine -- but any way, he played in our band. And another guy who was a trombone player with Benny Carter was also in our band, his name was Alton Moore. And these were real pros. And Montgomery, Handy -- at this time Handy would do tours, also. And he'd bring his band to Montgomery and all the guys would come to my house and I was just in awe of everybody there, you

know. These were real stars.
So I had just been engulfed in music, just surrounded by music all my life. Now, how I started playing guitar. I heard Eddie think I had Eddy Lang, and I made up my mind I was going to play, be a guitarist. And I really taught myself, because I would hear certain voicings on a guitar, and I would just fool with it until I got just the voicings I wanted, which was kind of unorthodox. And it took an awful lot of work, I guess it took years and years and years for me to develop, you know, the strength, I guess, to do these things.

And this is how I started. And my mother also at this time we left -- let's see, we left Montgomery, and we went to Chicago. This was around 1920 something, I was very small, you know. And I went to school in Chicago, and I went to school with Ray Nance. And -- who was a tremendous musician. We were in Wendell Wenda Philipps together. But Wendell Philipps High School. They had a very good band then. Nance had a very good band. I used to play with Nance's band, incidently.

But also I used to play house rent parties. This was during the Depression, and we would -- my mother would play these house rent parties, I would play, and Dan Grissom. We used to go -- we used to book house rent parties, and they'd have poker games, and whatever, you know, and they'd sell home brew and --
Did you get paid?
Oh, we got paid, yeah, we got paid. I was told musicians just got to eat and drink.
(Inaudible).
No, no, we got paid. We were booked, you know, we were that good. You worked the rent party circuit.
(Inaudible).

Yes, right. So any way, I used to do this, and I had mentioned Dan Grissom. But he used to sing like Louis Armstrong, and my mother stopped him from singing like Louis Armstrong, he made him stop -- he had such a beautiful voice. But any way, he was working with us when he went with Lunceford. My mother had a little trio in Chicago, so I -- I keep bringing my mother up, but she was such a tremendous pianist and she was such a hard taskmaster, because if I would play wrong, anything wrong, she might hit me or anything. She was just -- oh, but we were inseparable. And I really attribute most of how I feel about music to my mother. You know, there's nothing -- her taste was immaculate. And her playing as far as I was concerned was immaculate, and I was a pretty good judge because I heard everybody.

And she also -- while we were in Chicago she also worked for the Oriental Theatre. She used to do like a rehearsal pianist. At this time they wouldn't have a colored pianist in a band or anything, in a white band, but she did all the rehearsal work for the Oriental Theatre and the Chicago Theatre. She was a fine musician.

So I stayed there and struggled and thought, and it's -- you mentioned John Levy. I've got to tell you about John Levy. I -- my father was a postman, and he insisted that I go into the post office as a special delivery boy. I think I was around 16 years old then. But I wanted to play music, I didn't want to be in -- and I finally went down, just to appease my father, and that's where I met John Levy. This was in Chicago. John Levy was playing piano like Earl Hines, and he was a piano player. I think I was playing banjo.
Did you start on guitar or did you start on banjo?

No, I started on banjo -- I started on the ukulele. I'm getting ahead of my story. Actually, how I started playing a string instrument. My mother gave my sister, who also was a very fine pianist herself, marvelous pianist, she gave her a ukulele. And I took it and played it. My sister never could play it and I just took it and just played it. And this is how I think this is the beginning of the string instrument for me. From there I just -- I went to a banjo and I heard Eddie Lang and I made up my mind then that I was going to play guitar.

But the thing of it is nobody taught guitar then. You couldn't get a teacher. They -- everybody was groping, they didn't know too much about it themselves, so you just had to have some ingenuity and imagination, I should say, and do

these things yourselves. So this is why I had to teach myself. But even if I had had a teacher, I always heard certain sounds and I would have to voice the chords a certain way or else it would just bug me. So this is why my fingering was a little different, and --
You heard things that you hadn't heard (inaudible). you wanted...
anyone else play, and listening to your mother (inaudible) little children?
That's right, that's right. And so I had to do them myself, and I would sit and just figure out how to get the voicing. This is what I wanted to hear.
Did this start happening when you were (inaudible) little children?

Yes. And I guess I'm really getting ahead of my story, but you know my mother used to have a choir in Montgomery, and I would have to go to choir practice with her. And I used to sit in the balcony of this empty church while they were practicing, you know, rehearsing, on stage. And I used to hear all kind of sounds. They would sing certain kind of tunes, or songs, and I would sing just something contrapuntal to that, by myself. And I would hear different voices and I would go on a tangent from where they were going.

And I just always heard like this, you know. So as I say, it was just a gift, I guess, you know. But coming back to Charlie Christian, I heard Dizzy say -- Dizzy's the only one who really tells the truth about -- I don't say tell the truth. Who really is aware what happened. I never tried

to play like Charlie Christian. I've been given credit for playing like Charlie or being influenced by Charlie, but I never -- I always admired his playing, he was a tremendous guitarist. But we thought differently, and I would go to hear Charlie every night in Minton's. That's when Dizzy was there, and Joe Guy and Monk. Let's see, the bass player was Nick Finton, and the saxophone player's name was Scotty.

And every night I would go there because Charlie would come by and play, and I admired his play. But I never wanted to play like him, because I heard different things, you know. His was a very exciting style and everybody just loved him, including me. And all the guitarists just jumped on his style. But I had to be me, and I guess I'm stubborn, you know. But I'm still getting a little ahead of my story because I want to tell you when I first met Charlie I had been on the road with Fletcher Henderson, and I'll get to a story about Fletcher. But I had been on the road with Fletcher Henderson and I got in town this night and I went to Monroe's Uptown House. And Charlie was playing, and I had my guitar and I started chording and playing for him, and he turned around and he stopped playing and he stopped and looked at what I was doing, because I was -- he liked what I was doing. You know, this was how I met him.
But it was a mutual admiration thing. But
MS. WILLARD: It wasn't Like (inaudible) Leonard Feather's Encyclopedia of Jazz says, when he calls you Christian - inspired.
No, no, I -- listen, always Leonard -- you know, I love him but sometimes I question some of the things he says, especially about me, and my age.
He said you were underrated. (inaudible).

Yeah, he said, but I'm over age. But any way, I never was -- I never tried to play like Charlie, still don't. But now, I told you that I was with Fletcher Henderson. I went to New York -- after my mother died I went to New York to live, 1938, '39, some time ago, '40. 1940. I had been to New York previously with Roy Eldridge. And this is really when I met Dizzy, was in 1937, at the Savoy Ballroom, when I was there with Roy Eldridge. But I went back in 1940 to live, and someone told me, I think Sid Catlett or someone told me that Fletcher was having auditions for guitar player.

Now, I knew that if I told him who I was I would have had the job automatically, you know, because my mother was very good friends. She had introduced me to him at the Savoy Ballroom in Chicago quite a few years before but he wouldn't have remembered me. So fine. So I went to audition for this job, and I never told him who I was, and I got the job, incidently, and I worked with him about six months before I told him who I was. We were riding on the bus one day in Mississippi or someplace, and I said, Fletcher, you really don't remember where I met you. He said, no, John. I said, well my mother, Georgia Garham. And he died, you know. Why

didn't you tell me? But I had to get the job this way. Now, we'll go back again. I told you that I went to New York for the first time with Roy Eldridge. I worked with Roy. When he left Fletcher he formed a band, this was in '36. And I worked with Roy, I was in his band in Chicago, the Three Deuces. We had a tremendous band. But before that I had worked at the Three Deuces at Tatum for about two years. Now, this was --
(Inaudible).

Yes, yes. The first solo I ever had on a recording was with Art, something called Battery Bounce, I believe. We made the Wee Baby Blues and the Battery Bounce and all this. This was the -- it was unamplified guitar, incidentally, all, But, I worked with Art every night for about two years, and he heard me with my mother's trio. He came by the place I was working, and I wasn't even in the union. And he told me that he had a job for me, to get in the union. So I got in the union, I went to work with him at the Three Deuces. And I said, I had never heard anything like this in my life. Art Tatum would line all the piano players, Alec Templeton, Horowitz, however, they would all come into hear Art Tatum. And the place was crowded, just packed, and they were lined against the wall listening to Art. And I'm sitting here absorbing this for two years, and I had never heard anything -- it just overwhelmed me. And I think I really

started grasping some of it, or knowing what I had learned after I left -- after he left, you know. And I used to play things that I had -- I tried to play some of the things that I heard him playing, voicings and things like that. And this was a tremendous training for me,--you know, just can you imagine. And then after we got off at night we -- in the morning, rather -- at night. When we got off at 4:00 o'clock in the morning then we'd go to an after hours spot.
You and Tatum.

Me and Tatum and a saxophone player by the name of Scoops Carey. And we'd go and we'd hang out, in an after hours spot. And he'd drink this beer and let every piano player in town play before he sat down. And when he sat down to play he wiped everyone out, you know. But this is --
Did you play with him then (inaudible).

At the after hours, no, I -- then I'd listen, I'd just sit here and listen. As a matter of fact the first time -- he introduced me to Billie Holiday. She came to Chicago to work the Grand Terrace, and we met her, our first night there we met her in the after hours spot and we hung out that morning until about -- that day until about 12:00 o'clock the next day just playing and just having a ball, you know.
But any way, I -- after Art left, Roy left Fletchers.
Roy was at the Grand Terrace with Fletcher Henderson, he and Chu Berry. So Roy formed this band that I was in Roy's band.

Gosh, I can't tell you, I stayed there for three years with Roy, I imagine. And that was a tremendous band. No, we had about six -- let's see, four rhythm, and three horns. Roy Eldridge, Dave Young playing tenor, and Scoops Carey playing alto saxophone. Tremendous alto saxophone player.
We stayed here at the Three Deuces, oh, for about three years.
(Inaudible).

Old Zut. And Cozy Cole's brother, Ted Cole, and Truck Parham, the bass player, tremendous bass player. And very good band. And all the musicians, anybody who was anybody would come to the Three Deuces. That all the travelling bands when they came to town, they would -- all the travelling white bands. No black was allowed in the joint at this time. Well, it was very prejudiced -- Chicago was a very prejudiced town, you know. So --
(Inaudible).

State and Wacker. Wacker Drive and State Street, in the basement. But no black musicians could come there, you know, clientele, no patrons, black patrons could come there. They'd get run out of there. This was Chicago at that time. It was a terrible -- Chicago really started -- I think the blacks started the upheaval, I should

say, during the war, World War II. But up until that time there were many restaurants that you couldn't go into, you know, they wouldn't serve you. Hotels. You couldn't stay -- Chicago was a terribly prejudiced town. But any way, they had some good bands.

At this time, when I was working at the Three Deuces with Roy, all -- as I said, all the musicians came in. That's -- oh, just Red Norville, Mildred Bailey, their band of just all the great bands. So it was kind of a showcase, and we had a very good band, and we were broadcasting from there. Basie had a little six piece band or seven piece band that was broadcasting from Kansas City at the time, and they came on just before, so we would sit in the car and hear them, and then when they'd go off we'd rush in and we'd start broadcasting. And Fats Waller would bring his whole band in and jam with us, this is the truth. They had a big band, they had a 16 piece band and he'd have them lined all around the tables. He would bring his whole band in and jam, on the bandstand. I said no black musicians came in there. That's not true. Shuberry would come in. On the stands some nights would be Shuberry, Ben Webster, Lester, they all at the same time. Don Byas. This is in Chicago now, this is before New York.
(Inaudible).
This was with -- Lester was with Basie.

They left Kansas City and they came to the Grand Terrace. This was their first trip out of Kansas City. This was a trip before -- this was the engagement, rather, before they went to New York. They were on their way to New York then. They had a guitar player with them then, incidentally, by the name of -- oh, gosh, I can't remember his name. He played violin also. But it wasn't Freddy Green. I think his name was Williamson, something else. I'll think of it. But a very good guitarist. And played violin, fiddle like Stuff. That style.

But any way, they would come down and Count Basie would come to the club in a raincoat, and it was 10 below zero. They were that poor. But any way, tremendous -- musically it was just something else. Chy Choo, Ben, you know, Prez, it was -- they were all different. But they ---
Rewarding (inaudible).
Yeah, just all night long we just jammed. It was just a most rewarding experience, and good, you know.

Zutty left and we had another drummer by the name of Doc Young -- no, Doc West, Harold West, who was a very fine drummer. You've heard of West. Yeah. So he played with us for quite a while, and then I -- this is the first time I went to New York was with Roy Eldridge. We played the Savoy. At this time Paul Whiteman had acclaimed claimed Roy the world's greatest trumpet player.
And the only trumpet player -- well, we played oppo-

site Erskine Hawkins. He had in the Savoy Ballroom in New York, and Roy would just wipe him out every set, you know, it was just pitiful. Erskine had this band and we'd come on and we were the foot stompers, you know. But the only trumpet player that would come up with -- and jam with Roy was a guy by the name of Dizzy Gillespie. And he played different from anyone.
I noticed this harmonic sense was different -- he was harmonically different from anything I'd ever heard, you know. And he would come and jam on the stand with Roy.
In the Savoy?

In the Savoy, and I would say well this guy here is something else, you know, because as I say, just the mere fact that he was acclaimed the greatest trumpet player in the world, and Roy was very exciting, you know. But never phased Dizzy at all. He'd barge right in with his innovations and he was innovative, believe me. You know, this is why people talk about who the daddy of bebop and the daddy of this. It was Dizzy Gillespie, nobody else.
Well, Dizzy says that it was an interchange of ideas.
Yes.
Among him and Bird and Clarke and you.
Yes, but this was before Bird. See, this is before --
Where are we now, 1940?

We are at 1938. This was before Bird. Bird hadn't -- he was still in Kansas City, we hadn't heard anything of Bird then. As a matter of fact, I went to New York around '40 and I lived at the Woodside Hotel. Bird was selling pot. I didn't even know Bird played saxophone. We used to call him the Shadow because Bird would wear this dark cap and this long black overcoat, and he was a man, you know. He sold pot.

So one day I was going to rehearsal with Roy, and Bird Burt was there, and I asked him to come on and go to rehearsal with me. You know, so he went around, allegedly to sell some pot. He -- at this time Joe Eldridge was playing with Roy, Roy's brother. Very good saxophone player. And someone asked Bird Burt, they knew him, and asked him to play. And we never rehearsed. When Bird Burt got through blowing that was just it. I was the most amazed person in the world. I didn't know Bird played the saxophone. I knew him as a man.

Then he started going to Monroe's uptown house, and playing and he got to be known there. And then he worked with Jay McShan. But now I knew Dizzy -- this was before Dizzy, I mean this -- Dizzy was before Bird. In my, you know -- differently than anyone, MS. WILLARD: Dizzy played (inaudible). MR. COLLINS: Yes, yes. And records will prove it. All you've got to do is just play some of the records that
Dizzy was --
Eldridge phase, (inaudible).
He had already gotten through his
Yeah.
Dizzy originally played like Roy.

Yeah, well you see Roy and Dizzy knew eachother. Well, they knew eachother, they'd played before I ever went to New York, before Roy came to Chicago with Fletcher Henderson. So I didn't know anything about Dizzy, you know. And all I knew that all the trumpet players tried to play like Roy. Everybody but Dizzy.
Dizzy said he did and went on from (inaudible).
there.

Well, yeah, yeah, possibly. But when I got to New York the scene had changed, as far as Dizzy is concerned, and Roy. But it was always different. He was a true individual musically, you know, he had his own ideas. And we used to jam all the time. He'd come up to my hotel room and we would just play and exchange ideas, and then we used to go to another hotel called the Grampion. Now, who's living there? Ben Webster. And the three of us would play, we'd just sit there all day and just play, and exchange ideas. And I always thought Ben was -- what can I say, exquisite. He's beauty, he's just sheer beauty, you know.
So I really got to know Dizzy, musically and
otherwise. And as I say he was -- I always admired him because he was -- you had to put him over there. He was different. But any way, let me take a breather. Okay? [pause in tape]

Are we back? Good. Speaking of Dizzy, I was working with Benny Carter at the Three Deuces, and he needed a trumpet player and I recommended Dizzy. I don't think Benny was really aware of Dizzy, but any way he hired Dizzy and the band was just tremendous. How I started working with Benny, at -- I think it was Kelly's Stables. I had been working, as I told you, with Fletcher Henderson, and man, we had been on the road, I'd been to Tupelo below Mississippi to two above Mississippi, two aside Mississippi. I was just so sick of Mississippi and all of the places. And we came back to Chicago, we had about a five day layoff, and I decided to go to New York, for the five days.

And I went to New York, and Nat Cole -- I hadn't seen Nat in years because when I went to New York he went to California so I didn't see him, but I had heard about what he was doing. But any way this was -- now, this had to be in 1941, around 1941, so at the Kelly's Stables Nat Cole was appearing, and also Benny Carter's band. So I went in and I heard Nat's group, and it was just beautiful. I just loved it, you know, and it -- I was also glad to see him, and surprised to hear him sing, you know, because Nat and I had vied for jobs around Chicago, these little gigs, and he was --

Nat was a tremendous pianist, he was a genius on this piano. But I never knew that Nat could sing, you know. When I heard him sing it was just something, and I would -- and Benny's band was good, and it was just good to get out of Mississippi. And Benny had a guitarist with him, a very good guitarist from Cleveland by the name of Willie Lewis. He was blues oriented. That was his background.

But any way, they had some argument or something, and I don't know whether Benny fired him that night or he quit, but any way Benny asked me to come with the band. So I got on the phone and called Fletcher in Chicago and told Fletcher that I wanted to stay, and Fletcher begged me to come back and I'd say Fletcher, you just can't do this to me, I'm so tired of the road and so and so and so and so. But if you insist. He said, well, John, if you just want to stay there, okay.

So I stayed in New York and went to work with Benny. And let's see now, who was on this bill? I think it was Benny Carter, and Nat, and his trio, Art Tatum, and we had a singer by the name of Miss Rhapsody. She didn't call herself Miss Raspody-- Rhapsody, it was Miss Raspody, you know. And I think this whole show cost him around $900.00 a week, you know. This was just the --
Was Nat (inaudible).
Nat's trio.
Nat's trio. (inaudible).
Tatem was doing a single.
And then Benny had (inaudible).

Let's see, Benny had four rhythm and three horn. A baritone saxophone, a trumpet and Benny played alto and trumpet, or whatever. You know, whatever he felt like playing. He played everything, you know. But a beautiful experience. And after we left there Benny formed a bigger band and I worked with him then, and we went to the Apollo Theatre, and this is where I got my greetings from Uncle Sam. And Benny -- I was so upset, and so Benny said, well John, look, I'm going to go before the board with you. And Benny went before the board with me to try to get me out of the army and they almost got Benny. We laugh about this now, but I left Benny Carter's band to go into the army.

But in the mean time Art had approached me about joining him with the trio, but you know, obviously I couldn't take the job because I had to go into the army, so I came back to New York on furlough and I went to see Art. He was working at this time at another club now, the Three Deuces, farther down the street. And this was in 1942. And Tiny Grimes was playing with him. And Art would tell me, John, please go over there and teach Tiny "Body and Soul", but Tiny was -- he just loved Charlie Christian, this is all he knew was Charlie Christian. He didn't know anything about chords or

voicings or anything, so I would show him these tunes. Every time I would go to New York I would have to do this, you know, and it would kill me because I wanted to be out of the army. But it seemed, you know -- you wonder why I never got more acclaim.

Now, this is why -- as fate would have it, I was just in the wrong place at the -- you know, when things were happening -- when something would happen that I would just be off the scene, you know. I spent four years in the army, you know. This is right at the time when I should have been doing good things, you know.
Well, was there any guitar player that was getting any attention up until Christian (inaudible). (Came along?)
Well, Floyd Smith was with Andy Kirk's Crook's band. He was getting a little acclaim. But Christian came along, and with his electric guitar and that --
Well Dizzy, it was the first time anybody (inaudible). had ever been able to hear the guitar.
That's right.
And that's when people became more aware of the instrument.

Well -- so any way, now I'm going to go back a little farther again. I'm going a little -- let's see, when I went to New York to live I worked with Roy Eldridge at the Areadia Ballroom. He had a big band, a good band.

And we left there, we got a small group and we went to -- we went to Kelly's Stables, which was on 51st Street then I believe. And this is when I first met Leonard Feather, when he first came over. And I -- if I'm not mistaken Leonard was married at that time to a piano player. I'm sure he was.
Leonard's been married twice.
(Inaudible).

Yes. I knew his first wife. Yeah. But any way, we went to Kelly's Stables, 51st Street, and let's see who was appearing there then? The Harlem Highlanders. Baby Lawrence, and who almost literally danced up the wall. Oh, they had a tremendous group. Baby Lawrence, they had a guitar player by the name -- his name was Snaggs from Detroit, and another singer, a very talented guy that played bass. His last name was Glover, I don't remember his first name. But so talented.

But we stayed here quite a while, at the Kelly's Stables there. This is when all the pimps and all the hustlers would hang out there. You'd see all the prostitutes. They would bring -- the madams would bring all the girls in and set them around the table. And I could tell you some stories about Jackie Gill, our old favorite. You remember Jackie Gill? This is when I met Jackie Gill. He was one of the boys.
But any way, this was Kelly's Stables then, and Leonard was coming around then and Georgia All, so now here we go. Benny Goodman had Charlie with him at this time. This

is my reason for telling you this now. Benny was auditioning another band, and Georgie All had been coming around with -- playing with us, jamming with us all the time at Kelly's Tables. And he was -- Benny was looking for a rhythm guitarist. I had a friend then who was in New York, a white guy by the name of Mike Bryan. He was from Memphis. A very good guitarist. And I recommended Mike for the job. I was working with Roy, I was having such a ball I really wasn't interested.

So Mike got the job, and he and Charlie became very good friends. Charlie was a feature guitarist. And Charlie gave Mike a guitar and an amplifier. Well, Mike did not play electric guitar, so Mike in appreciation for my getting him the job, gave me the guitar, Charlie's guitar, and amplifier. It's the first electric guitar and amplifier I ever had. So this is why I started playing, and Roy would argue with me all night long. He didn't want to hear the amplified guitar, and I would play it anyway, you know. But he wasn't accustomed to hearing anything like that and he just wanted to hear the natural guitar.
But this -- the first electric guitar and amplifier was Charlie Christian's, through Mike Bryan.
had play jazz electric guitar, Charlie Christian was the first to (inaudible).
(inaudible).
Well, no. There was another guy before him by the name of Eddy Durham. Eddy Durham was a trombone player from Kansas City. I forgot who Eddy played with. He
(Busic)
played very good guitar, and trombone, and he was a writer. But he was the first one with the amplified guitar. Yes. After him, Charlie.
When did you hear Eddie Durham?
(inaudible).

Well, this was before I left Chicago. He was with -- I think he -- who was he with? Some band out of Kansas City. And then he was with Luncford for a while. I'm almost sure he was with Luncford for awhile.. But anyway this is how I got my first electric guitar. We've touched sort of lightly on Art Tatem. I know you were with him on two different occasions. The first time I think was for two years in Chicago. But we haven't really talked at any great length about Tatem. What was he like?

Well, he was very fine person, a great -- as we know he's a great musician, and a great card player. You know, he's had -- I would say he -- he wasn't totally blind, he -- let's say, I would say he was 90 percent blind though. But he could -- he had a photographic memory, and we would play -- when we were at the Three Deuces in Chicago we -- he loved to play cards, and we would play the boss, Sam Beards, and whoever, and Art and I would always team up. And Art would remember every card that hit the board, you know, he would take it up and put it very close to his eyes to see what the number -- you know, what card it was. He remembered what everyone played, and -- in other words we never lost.

We would drink so much we couldn't work sometimes -- I couldn't, he could. But he -- you know, because Art loved to drink, as you know. And drink or smell, that's what we would call him. So they would smell and buy and we would drink.

But he loved to play cards, and when we -- he was a great pinochle player. When we had the trio with Slam Stewart and Art and myself, now this was just before I joined Nat Cole, he and Slam would just play pinochle all night long. He wouldn't let -- Slam was almost a captive. He couldn't get out, you know, he couldn't get away from Art after the job. He just had to play cards.

And he was a little -- I don't know whether I said this before but when I ---he really didn't want me to join Nat because we had quite a good thing going. And I was under contract to him. I might have mentioned this before, but he finally said, okay, John, if you must go, because Nat was pretty good and making quite a bit of money at that time. And this was a step, financially for me, you know, a step forward financially for me. But musically where do you go from Art?

But any way, I wondered about it. I left him in St. Paul, Minnesota. I flew to California and joined Nat at the Tiffany Club, and I wondered how Art really felt about it. I knew he was a little peeved with me, and with Nat, but as soon as he came to California I looked up at night and there he was in the Tiffany to see. Because -- to see us. He loved Nat and he loved me. So every night he was there and when he became ill he stayed home quite a bit. And he had a chauffer by the name of -- he used to call him Chicken, and he had Chicken to bring him by my hotel every

day and I would have dinner with him at Mike [Limens.] And I felt so sorry because he was just a shell of his former self. He would come up to my hotel room and just sit and I can remember Ben Webster, Harry Edison Addison, Dan Grissom Grisom, we would all lie and do everything, just stand on our heads just to make him laugh. And he -- because he had a hell of a sense of humor. But at this point we really couldn't get to him. I didn't --
Was he still playing then when --

I don't believe -- the only thing he was doing then, Norman Granz Grands was astute shall I say, he was hip enough to realize that he wasn't going to live, I guess, so he had him to come into the studio and do quite a bit of recording during that time. And I was out of town when he died. But --
That recording was the solo piano pieces.

That's right. Norman recorded him right at that time. But he was very ill, you know. But when he bought his first home here in View Park, which was quite a thing -- I don't think there were any blacks at all. He came by and got me up and took me up here to see his new home, and I always believed that Paul [Gadden] bought that home after Art sold it you know -- when he died I think his wife just sold it and I think she sold it to Paul. Paul Gidden.
But any way, Art loved piano players, as you know, and we were working together, another time, in New York at Cafe

Society downtown. And during the intermission we would drive uptown, say we had a bottle, and had two hours off. We would drive uptown to a little club of a friend of his, Tom Tillman, who owned this club, the Hollywood Club, and we would go up here to listen to the beetle -- these are stride piano players.
Who?

Or whoever was there. What was this guy's name? Marlowe Morris. Was a great stride piano player. So we would go up here between shows, and we'd have the chauffeur to drive us back down to finish. After that he would -- we would go to another place -- when we finished work rather we would go to another club called Rubens. Now, you understand that I was always with him. Okay. We would go to Rubins.

Now, this is a place we -- you go in the building and you go down a flight of stairs to the basement, and you go through a tunnel to another building, and then a little room. I think the floor plan -- say like a 9 by 12 rug, you get in there. There's Teddy Wilson, Chittison, Herman Chittison, just all of the piano players waiting for Art.
(Inaudible).

This was in Harlem. This was in Harlem, I forget, it was around 132 or somewhere around there. But this -- I remember this place, it was called Rubens. And we would go in here and they would all play. And when they finished, Art would wipe everybody out. Just -- and then in

the meantime he's drinking beer, always drinking this beer, you know. At one time he just used to drink quite a bit of whiskey but I think towards the last he was just drinking beer. But he was there drinking until everybody finished and he loved everybody's playing, you know, but then came the thunder, you know. It was just beautiful. This is what they were waiting for. They wanted to hurry up and get through so they could hear him play. They knew he would not play until they had finished. And he would just play for hours.

Nothing, just Scott Joplin's wife. This is all he said, John, we're going to Scott Joplin's wife. She had a nice apartment, and we'd go up here and he'd buy drinks and he would play. chords, you know, one, three, five chords. And Art would upset him so badly sometimes, so Art would tell me, 'Say, watch, John, watch what I'm going to do.' So he would start playing 'Danny Boy.' We used to go -- we used to go to track meets, you know.

in some year, and he's telling me while he's playing, the batting champ, so and so and so and so. It was Joe Dimaggio. And he was right. And we played back this recording that he made and it was a masterpiece. It's just he had that kind of mind, you know.

So it was quite an experience being with him, and as I say I felt very closely -- I was very close to him, you know, and I was very, very, very fond of him. You know. But I left and went to the army, you know.
It was right before you went into the army.
Yeah, that's right. And as I told you, I

And --

Yes, it is.
You know. So that was why --

Oh, yes. All the pianists of classical and jazz, they knew Art Tatum.

You mentioned something about Fats Waller and his band, but --

Oh, okay. Art often told me the story of he was appearing with Adelaide Hall as her accompanist, and Fats was on the same bill with this band. And Fats took him to New Jersey to meet a guy by the name of Donald

Lambert, who was supposed to be the king of the stride piano. And Art said that the guy really could play. I finally got a chance to meet Donald Lambert once. They did one of these jazz festivals or something, at WNEW. They used to have them yearly in New York, and Donald Lambert was there and I met him, and he could play. Stride piano. But Art was the master.
Art kind of liked to I'd like to kind of wait until everybody was through and then cut everybody down. I've heard stories about that.
Yes, yes.
I heard one here in Los Angeles, where he and Peterson --
Yeah.
-- were playing, alternating all evening, and it was supposed to be an even contest so Art went in and played "Little Man" said (inaudible) You've Had a Busy Day.

one, no. But he knew that once he played the piano players wouldn't play, and he wanted to hear them also. But what could they play after he finished? You know, he was very humble, you know, it wasn't that. He knew that he was the president, I'm sure, but then he also knew that after he finished what could they play. So he had to wait until everybody -- he had to let everybody play and then play.

Now, I -- it's just -- one thing I want to say is for the young musician we have some fine young musicians now, on all instruments. That's piano, drums, guitar, trumpet, whatever. But for them I think they should realize that what they are doing now is essentially an extension of what has been done before. And they should all go back just dig and listen to what was done before, and see how great the musicians of these different eras were and what they really contributed. You know. Because these musicians now -- I'm sure a lot of them think that they are creating and, you know, what they are doing has not been done before, and they forget. But if they will listen to some of the recordings of some of the things that were done before, they would see that it has been done before.

In other words kind of check up on the heritage, you know. I am very -- as you know, as I told you before -- chord conscious. But I have a -- you mentioned something to me that I had forgotten about working in Chicago with Elbert Topps.

Now, that was a club called the Radio Inn, I believe it was on 18th Street, and it was an after hours spot, and so on and so on. But I remember a guy came in one night who was there obviously with a show. He was a black guy, and his name was Putney Dandridge. This man made a tremendous impression upon me because he played piano and he had such beautiful bass lines. I had never heard this before.

Now, this guy -- I don't know, I haven't heard too much of him -- and I'm sure that there's a history, you know, a record of him, someplace. Putney Dandridge. But this guy had the most beautiful bass line on piano and it fascinated me. I never forgot it. And it influenced me quite a bit because I saw the beauty, you know. My mother always tried to tell me this, but here was a guy and I saw it with someone else. And he was a tremendous pianist. You see, but now the writers and the players now are very aware of bass lines, but this was done even then.
Then you mean --
Oh, this was in the thirties, this was in the early thirties, you know.
Do you remember what show he was in?
I never knew. Only thing I remembered about him was his name. Because he impressed me that much. But there was Jelly Roll Morton, and J. P. Johnson, all of these were tremendous pianists. And they --
Did you hear them?

I heard records of them, I didn't hear them in person. I heard Putney Dandridge, but these records, if you listen you'll see how much they contributed and how similar some of the things they're doing -- they were doing then are to the things that the guys are doing today. You know. And saxophone, like Lester Young was different, but he always reminded me of a guy that played with Paul Whiteman, Frankie Trombar. And then talking to him in later years he was influenced by Frankie Trumbauer, he told me. You know. And so now from Lester came Alan Eager, Stan Getz, all of these. So this is just an extension of what had been done. I'm taking you down the line now, you know, from Frankie Trumbauer, Lester, Stan Getz, and so forth. See, this is -- So they should really -- I mean go and listen to what is -- to some of the older musicians, what have been done before.

No, he mentioned -- it was so -- I liked Frankie Trumbauer so much, myself, and I broached the subject to him because I saw the similarity. Because there was just a plain quality to Frankie Trumbauer's playing that always kind of grabbed me. Something a little different. And I recognized the same thing in Lester's playing. And finally I asked him and he told me that he was influenced by Frankie Trumbauer.

But, as I said, this is to show you how these things go right down the line. So that is where it all began, you know, and I think that they should kind of check back, you know, and -- see, now, as I told you, the first black guitarist that I heard, that really should I say influenced me was Eddie Durham. And he was a trombonist, but a marvelous guitarist, and there was another one and I can't think -- here's another trombonist. His name was Coffee and he played very fine guitar. I'm trying to think whose band he was with, and I can't remember. His last name was Coffee. It seemed as if all the trombone players were playing guitar then.

But as I say, this -- the kids should really look back and see, you know, go back and listen to what was happening. And on guitar a lot of them are, because a lot of them are listening to Christian, you know. But it didn't -- who was Christian influenced by. See, this is -- someone told me and Led Belly I forgot. Oh, it wasn't Led Belly. I forget who it was, it'll come to me in a moment. But these are the things that I would advise them to do.
You've got some interesting looking notes there. What are they?

No, I just -- I wanted to mention Sidney Bechet who was one of the great saxophonists, you know, and a lot of the musicians aren't aware of how great he was. He was with Noble Sissle's band, and I used to go to see them

quite often. And here was a man that was a giant. Also in that same band, playing bass, was Eddie Cole, Nat's brother, who also played piano. You're aware of Eddie Cole. But he was a bass player with that band. Noble Sissel had just returned from Europe, and this was the first time I'd really got a chance to see Bechet in person and here was a giant who had contributed so much. You know, he had such a unique style, and he played soprano saxophone which was just beautiful, you know.
And then there was -- what can I say, but like Benny Carter. These -- here was another giant whose style was altogether different. A very cultured style, you know, very schooled, warm.
And also he was a master of quite a few instruments.
Quite a few instruments. Trumpet, yes, piano.
All the saxophones, piano.
Yeah, yeah. But these -- I think the kids should check up on -- go back and see what these guys have contributed and listen to what they did. Because as I say Bechet was a true giant.
He was, I think, one of the four musicians that Duke always cited as being the most important.
Yes.
Musicians in jazz history, (2nd) one of his principal influences.

Yeah. I heard the trumpet players now doing Freddy Hubbard and a lot of the things that he does reminds me of Rex Stewart. You see, Rex Stewart was a great trumpet player, he was an innovator, you know, and a lot of the things that the trumpet players are doing now, and especially Freddy Hubbard, reminds me of what Rex Stewart was doing then. And I'm sure that Freddy's probably aware of this, you know, but so much of this has been done that the average student or young musicians now aren't aware of. And I think they should be, whatever their particular instrument is, you know. They should kind of dig back and -- delve back and see where it came from. And it'll be so enlightening, and beneficial to them.
In going back through our tapes so far, there are a few things I wanted to ask you. You mentioned your grandmother, and she was a very good pianist.
Yes.
What was her name?
Mary Jane [Gorhan].
Mary Jane [Gorhan.] Okay.
You know, I tell you, I went to see a movie -- she was a great woman, you know, she was a very fine singer, also. I went to see a movie, the sneak preview

of a movie called "Mandango" or something. Have you heard of this book? But any way, it's about slaves. And the treatment of slaves, and how the white man handled the slaves after that they were brought over here. And my grandmother was a slave as a little girl, and I was very hostile when I came out of this movie because everything she had told me I saw in this movie.
What kind of --

And how they separated families, they separated children from their mothers. And sent -- sold them to other plantation owners. And my grandmother was born in Georgia, and how they sold her to someone in Alabama, and she never saw her mother, any of her relatives any more. when she was sold?
How old was she (inaudible).

Oh, she was just a little girl. You I don't know. But how she -- the master's daughter, who's taking piano lessons, and she was what they called the house nigger, I guess, you know, she was her companion. And she would be right there when she was taking these lessons, and she learned to read and to play piano by watching her -- this little girl, her mistress, I guess, mistress' daughter, take piano lessons. And my grandmother really had the talent, you know, so she developed from there.
But I saw this movie and it just was -- it just tore me up. But here we go again. From there came your rhythms,

you know, the African rhythms, because as we all know, the Africans are very musical and very rhythmic. Yeah. So it was just ironic that I should go and hear and see this movie and all of this flashed back to me. I think half of the people in there, most of the people in there were hostile when they came out. You know, but musically this is how my grandmother started playing.
So she taught music, as I told you, also, and so did my mother. But my mother was quite talented also.
You said that your mother played in one church and your grandmother in another.
Yeah, yeah.
What were the churches? Do you remember any of the churches?

Well, one was Old Ship Church. That was an AME Church, African Methodist Episcopal, and my grandmother played in Mount Zion. That was a Baptist church. So that meant that I had to go to choir practice at both churches. The young men's Christian endeavor, and the BYPU, and oh, boy, and that fire and brimstone really got me. But --
BYPU, Baptist --
That's right, yeah.
Baptist Youth what?
Prayer --
Union?

-- Union, I imagine, yes. And the Methodist was a Young Men's Christian Endeavor. Yes, so it was the same thing, just different name. But any way, that was the south at that time. That's what most of the black musicians -- that's the way they performed. You know, this was their outlet, yes. So you got -- your blues came from there, because I hear some of these gospel churches now, I'm sure you hear them on the air, and it's all blues, you know. But this is their way of expressing themselves.
Do you remember any other stories from your grandmother about music?
Well, this was just the source for musical education.
Was there music amongst the slaves, or (inaudible). Were they allowed to go to church, did they have their own kind of --
Yes, they went to -- they had their own little church, they had their own services. They weren't allowed to participate because they weren't allowed to read or write. That was against the law.
Did they -- were they able to associate with eachother?
With eachother, yes.
They had their churches or --
Yes, it was more of a clandestine thing.

But as you know it was against the law for them to read or write, so when she -- she had to practice the piano, you know, on the QT. You know, but she was a student to retain to absorb rather some of the -- most of the lessons.

So any way, she married and after they freed them, I think when Sherman marched through the South they freed the slaves, and she married, you know, my grandfather and had quite a few children. But the one that was most musical was my mother. And she went to -- my mother was in Chicago during the time that King Oliver was there, but I was still in Montgomery with my grandmother. So she came back and she -- as I told you she taught music and at Selma, at Paine College there. And I went to Selma with her. This is where she formed this band. But we left, luckily. We got out in time.

So that's really how it -- I started, you know. And through her I was exposed to just about everything. Because when she was in Chicago, evidently she made quite a name for herself, and then she was in New York, she made quite a name for herself there. But she sacrificed most of it because of her children. She had two to. We were with our grandparents. So she couldn't leave us there, she had to come back and forfeit that, you know, to come back and get us.
So I lived in Kansas City, Kansas. She was playing --

you know, during those times they had the silent movies, and they would have the organist to play during the movie, showing of the movie. My mother did this, she went to Kansas City and she worked. There was one theatre, I forget this theatre, but it was at 18th and Vine or someplace.
A good location.

Yeah, yeah. She played for a theatre there, and she also played for another theatre in Kansas City, Kansas. So I went to school in Kansas City, Kansas, and I was looking through a book the other day and I saw a name, Chauncey Downs. And I remember that my mother played with him at Excelsor Springs, Missouri, and they didn't have a drummer and I played drums and I had never played drums before in my life. But I played drums with Chauncey's band, and I had the opportunity to see him -- I only lived there for a little over a year, then we went back south. But I saw Chauncey once after that. He was living in Lansing, Michigan, and I was there with Roy Eldridge. And someone happened to mention his name and I went to see him and it was -- he remembered me, as the drummer.
Ever played drums then?
No, never played drums since my legs were -- it was very tiring, you know. I never played drums after that.

I don't know whether I mentioned this before, but my first trip to Europe, which was 1947, I went over with Slam Stewart, Errol Garner, and myself. This was a trio. It was -- I've seen it listed in some -- as some jazz critic is writing history of jazz, said it was Errol Garner's trio. It was not Errol Garner's trio, it was Slam Stewart's trio. Okay. So it was -- Howard McGhee had the band, and --
(Unintelligible).
Howard McGhee had what band?

He had a band. Okay, it was Errol Garner, myself and Slam. Slam Stewart Trio. Howard McGhee's band and Coleman Hawkins, it was his first time in Europe since the war, you know. He left because of the war, and this was his first trip, which was like a triumphal return, you know. And I know I mentioned that the singer there was Chippy Hill. She was a blues singer. Yeah. But the one thing that I remembered about that trip was how fanatical the French people were about jazz. Traditional jazz as opposed to bop.

Now, as you know Howard McGhee was a bebop. This is the bebop era. Of course our group spanned both eras, and so did Coleman Hawkins, but the main bone of contention was Howard McGhee's group, and we played at the Marini Theatre, it's right at the foot of the Champs Elysees. And Panassie had bought a block of seats and they came there to boo, and they would boo, you know. They actually came -- every concert they were there and they would whistle, boo, you know, because
of the bebop. And so I had another experience like that.

When I returned to Paris with Nat Cole, we were doing a concert at the Salle Pleyel, and we had a French group to come on before we came on, see. So they played a few tunes and the people didn't want to hear them, they wanted to hear Nat. And so they started booing the band, so the band stopped playing and booed the audience. You know. But Pannassié, as everyone knows, he's a strict traditionalist, you know. He opposes anything other than Dixieland, I imagine. This is where he's coming from. So everything else is taboo with him, see. Which is strange in that we all know, any intelligent person knows that here we go again about extensions. You know. Of course we recognize that they are very fine musicians who play Dixieland. We know that. There are some that I have always admired.

But things move on, you know, we progress. So I think it's very shortsighted on his part to, you know. But anyway, I got a chance to see Kenny Clark, again, on this trip because I remember -- I've known Kenny for years when he -- I think he was playing with Edgar Hayes when I first met Kenny somewhere. I was in Cincinnati with Roy Eldridge, playing the Cotton Club, and this is where I first met Kenny.
And then when I went to New York we became very good friends, as a matter of fact we played around, we did quite a bit of recording, with different groups. As a matter of fact I

think Kenny did some recording with Mildred Bailey too, during this time. But when I went to Europe I saw Kenny again. This is another time he'd left the -- I think this time he stayed though. No, he didn't either, he came back once again to the states to live. But at that time it was one -- in '47 he had left for good, you know. He got disgusted with America and the Jewish bebop as he called it, and went to Europe. But -- so I did some recording with Kenny over there, and I -- all I know it was for Nicole Barkley. I forget -- I think her label was the Blue Note also, wasn't it, or --
I'm not certain.
Any way, I did some recording over there because why I remember is because Kenny borrowed the money that I made that day and he never paid me. I got paid for the date and he borrowed it right there.
You and Kenny Clark and whom else was (Inaudible) on the date?

Oh, some of the guys in Howard's group. I forgot who it was. Some -- yeah. But Kenny as I said, Kenny was -- it was his date, I really believe it was his date. But it was for Nicole Barclay Barkley, and she was trying to get Errol to record for her then. I don't think he would, for personal reasons, you know. But he didn't record for her. But I'm sure that we did -- I know that we did some recordings during that time.

But Hawk as I said at this time, it was just tremendous his going back, because he was so well loved, in Europe. He was quite a big man there. And this was his first time back there. So they didn't boo Hawk. Neither did they boo us, but they would boo -- every time Howard McGhee played they would just boo because they just could not accept bebop.
(inaudible)
What about the rest of the audience how did they accept it?

They were very responsive, but he -- Panassi Panaci had enough seats there to kind of disrupt things for her, you know, for a while. But this is how fanatical they were about this. And it was kind of nice seeing Kenny because I had recorded with these, I guess they're all stars at that time. When I came out of the army. This was done in '46. This was called 52nd Street jazz, I believe, and this was a original recording of Kenny's tune "Epistrophy." And in the band was Fats Novarro Navarro, Kenny Durham Durham, Ray Abramson, Eddie Dr. Vertegull Divertiville, and Sonny Stiss Stiff, saxophone, and Bud Powell and Al Hall, guitar, and it was quite a good player. I had a nice little solo on that also.

And as I say, it was the first time I had seen Kenny since then, and during that time as I told you I did so many recordings with Jacquet Jacquet and Dizzy also. As a matter of fact one of them was "Muttin Leg" Mudden-Leg, with Illinois Jacquet Jacquet, and his orchestra. And in that band was Leo Parker and Sir Charles

Thompson, Joe Newman and Russell Jacquet, and J. J. Johnson, Al Lucas on bass on -- Shadow Wilson on drum, which was quite 'Ow' 'Oo Pop A Dum' a band. And I know that I did Owi and Ooh-Bopadomp, with Dizzy, yeah. And let's see, who was in this band. David Elman Burns, Simon Wright and Matthew McKay and Ray Orr was trumpet. Howard Johnson and John Brown, alto sax, and James Moore Moody and Joe Gales, tenor sax. Cecil Payne was in the band, baritone. And John Lewis, piano, Ray Brown, bass, Milt Jackson and Joe Harris, drums.

But you know, it's kind of difficult to remember all of the personnel because it's been so long, but during that era it was kind of nice in that I had been away in the army and when I came back I was thrown right back with the Beboppers. You know. So that was kind of gratifying to me, but I had done quite a bit of research and practicing because I was aware of what was happening, even though I was in the army. Because music had changed all together when I came -- it was strictly the swing era when I went in. When I came back it was bebop.
How did all this affect Lester Young?

I don't think Lester ever recovered, really. You know, because the scene had changed so, and the army had probably demoralized Lester. I never could understand how they could keep a man of Lester's temperament in the army. You know, it probably -- I'm sure emotionally and otherwise it really took its toll on Lester.
Blesh says in his book, and I know you don't necessarily agree with Rush, but that Lester was I believe court-martialed while he was in the army.
I wouldn't be surprised.

And spent part of his time in prison. Supposedly over his possession of a pain killing pill which had been given him legitimately by an army base doctor after some kind of medical treatment. But that it was a case of racism, really.
Sure.
And he was put away, locked up and according to Rush was never the same emotionally or physically (inaudible).
Well, I don't know what to attribute it to, because --
Was that your impression after he came out, that he was totally different, (inaudible).

Yeah, yeah. Well, something had happened to him when he came out. He seemed to have lost his fire, it seemed as if he was just burned out. You know, it wasn't the same Lester that I had known. And I attributed that to being in the army, and knowing Lester I just could never understand how they could keep him in the army because he wasn't psychologically or emotionally suited for this type of life. You know?
How exactly do you mean?

Well, in the first place regimentation, you know, he couldn't go for that at all. This I knew. And he -- Lester was a very -- he was an introvert in a lot of ways, and a lot of people just wouldn't understand Lester. You know, they wouldn't understand him, and wouldn't know how to deal with him. Square. When I say a square I mean someone naturally out of the music business, wouldn't understand him. And they could -- and they could destroy a person, you know, like with me. When I went in the army and I had to go through all this training and all of this, which I had never done anything like this in my life. And I would slip off in the morning before they all went to the -- to do maneuvers, and you know, take this training. I could go to the band barracks and go to sleep.

So I did an awful lot of extra duty for doing this. They used to really punish me and I'd have to walk with full field packs and all this. But I just wasn't cut out for this. So finally the band -- it was-- we had a sergeant major in there, master sergeant, rather, by the name of Barry Ellis. He prevailed upon the colonel to just transfer me to the band. So I went into the band. So we stayed there for quite a while, and towards the last part of my army stay I went to Oakland, California, and they put me into a port company.

Now, these people are laborers, so they -- I didn't -- I really
didn't understand the type of company I was in, which didn't mean too much to me any way because I assumed that they had a band and that I would be in the band.

So they called me up one morning and marched me down to a freight yard where there were 14 freight cars to be unloaded, and he was calling off squads of 10 and he called me off and I said, no, you have nine. You don't have 10 this time. So the guy said, fine, so it's all right with me. So we went back to camp and they called me into the office, and the commanding officer said, well you refused to do this work today. And I said, yes. He said, why. I said, well if you'll look at my record you'll see that I'm a musician and I've always -- ever since I've been in the army this is all I have done. I don't know anything about unloading any box cars. Can you imagine this.

But any way, he made me wash every window on Thanksgiving Day. I washed every window in that mess hall, I think, which -- I think it was 100 windows. But I went to the special service officer then. I did the duty and then I went to the special service officer and I told him. And I'm wondering how did I get in a company like this. And he sent for my records and he saw what was happening, so he transferred me to another camp in Oakland, and in the band was Benny Green, and you know, this was -- I'm home free now.
But this is what they can do to you if you don't
stand up for yourself. And Lester wouldn't.
Well, that's -- not only that, but Lester was stationed in the South, like (inaudible).

Yeah, yeah. Oh, yeah, he was in Alabama. I knew where he was. He was not too far from where I was. I was in South Carolina. But fortunately I was with -- I was in a training camp, which means that we were there primarily to entertain the troops. We would march them in, entertain them while they're there, and we'd march them out, and bring another group in. So I stayed there for quite a while, and I had a little group there also. So I was more fortunate than Lester. I think he was in a different type of camp.

In the sketch story he says that when they searched Lester's locker they found a picture of his white wife, and this was more than his commanding officer could stand. And that this had something to do with the court martial, although efforts to find the records of what he was court marshalled for have proved fruitless. That there is no record of what he was court marshalled for, yet he was put in the guardhouse (inaudible).
Yeah, the guard house. Yeah.
For a long period of time.
Yeah, well I didn't know anything about that. Only -- I only knew that when I saw him, in New York, after the war, he had changed. There was something -- he

seemed to have lost his fire, something had happened to him. And it occurred to me that the army really did this to him because Lester was, as I said, was not emotionally up to army life. You know. That--
Sort of a free spirit.

That's right. And I mean, this was just his way. It wasn't -- he wasn't capable of changing. Lester was very strong in his beliefs, and in his life style, you know. So they could destroy him. And something actually happened to him then, you know. So I played with him around New York a couple of times, after that, and he had many groups after that. But to me, I don't know, it was just never -- not quite the same. And incidently, during this -- right after I came out Kenny Clark introduced me to John Lewis. I think Kenny Clark really discovered John Lewis in the army in Europe someplace, I believe. Yeah. So we used to go around to John because John lived on 122nd Street, near 7th Avenue, and I lived on 122nd Street and Morningside, which was not too far. And we would go around to see John. I heard him play, I was very impressed, you know, with the simplicity of his playing, depth. He had a certain something, you know. And after that I played with John, with Dizzy. With Gillespie.
Well, John had that -- before the war John hadn't been in the -- in New York, had he?
No, I think he --
He was from (Inaudible) Albuquerque, originally.
Yeah, but I think Kenny persuaded him to come to New York.
Kenny found him in Albuquerque.
No.
He found him in the army.

In the army, yeah,yeah. So I think it was in Europe now, and I think this is what Kenny told me. You know. But this is the first time I met John. Then he went with Dizzy, and from there on, you know --
Did you play at Minton's before Charlie Christian arrived in New York?
Yeah, I used to go down there and play.
I heard Dizzy say you did. (Inaudible)
Yeah, yeah.
He said who was (Inaudible) playing at Minton's.

Sure, I used to go down there and play with them, you know. They had a nice little band there. It was Joe Guy, Monk, bass player Nick Fenton, who I got to work with us with Prez, also. And saxophone player by the name of Scotty. And it was like a hang out too, you know. We would go there, if you could get through the pimps. You know, they would always follow the musicians because of the chicks, you know.
The musicians drew the chicks and the chicks drew the pimps.
Then the chicks drew the pimps, you know, and they would try to take the chicks or whatever, you know. And we were primarily interested in playing any way.
You didn't like the chicks.
Loved them, but I mean they had their place, you know.
What was that?
Second. Second to the guitar. Second to Dizzy and Monk and Joe Guy, you know.
What about Scotty. Do you know his whole name?

You know, I can't think of Scotty's whole name, and Scotty was a tremendous saxophone player. He worked with Earl Hines after that for quite a while, and that's all we ever called him was Scotty. You know. But he just can't -- he's in San Francisco now, last time I saw him he was in San Francisco. But yes, I played at Minton's, yeah. Before and after.
Minton's-- Before you only Willie mentioned (inaudible) listening at
Yeah, well this was --
But Dizzy said you were part of the (inaudible) scene.
Well, I did but as I say, I would go down to listen because Charlie wouldn't be in there all the

time, you know, and whenever Charlie was going to be there I wouldn't listen any way because I loved to hear him play. You know, but I played at Minton's, the uptown House, at Monroe's uptown house, and -- because everybody went there. And I found -- I was listening to a record yesterday of Dinah, and it was -- the name of the tune was 'Where Are You.' That was the first recording I ever made and I made it with Mildred Bailey, in Chicago. That was one of the tunes I was trying to think of where you -- and she was quite -- that's another story. Mildred, she was quite a gal.
PAUSE
Well, I think you mentioned her. We're talking about Mildred Bailey.

Well, one thing, it was just a funny incident I was thinking about. Mildred loved Billie but Billie always had a thing against Mildred because evidently Billie's mother worked for Mildred at one time. I don't know as a maid or as a cook or something, you know. And Billie -- and I think Billie always resented this, you know. But Mildred loved Billie's singing, and used to go up to the Uptown House quite often, because she knew that Billie would be there.
You're talking about Billie Holiday.

Billie Holiday, yes. Naturally, is there any other singer? Yeah, would go up there to hear her. You know, she knew she would be in. And everybody would go up there. It was quite a place, you know. And as a matter of

fact, Billie as you know -- I don't know whether she married Monroe's brother or they were just living together, but he was the one allegedly who started her on dope, you know. And all the musicians hated him, you know. But he had been in Europe and I think the war drove him back to New York. And she fell in love with this guy, he was a very handsome guy, but obviously a pimp, you know.
It's so -- it's just funny how the singers, the black singers at that time were just attracted to these hustlers and pimps. I just can't imagine why. But --
Who else?

Who else? Well, most of the singers during that time were, you know, but any way, we were talking about Billie. But Jimmie Monroe, he came back and we noticed that Billie had -- we all smoked pot, but Billie had graduated and she just got away from us. Because she kind of like belonged to us or we belonged to her, I don't know. Kenny Edison Clarke, Sonny White, Freddy Greene, me, Harry Addison. You know, we all loved her, we all kind of felt very close to her, we'd protect her, you know.

And she got away from us through this, so everybody hated Jimmie Monroe because of what he had done to her. Then she and Joe Guy got together, he was a trumpet player, as I told you, and I really believe that she started Joe Guy on the heavy stuff, because I saw Joe later, when I told you that

I recorded with them in San Francisco, and he was obviously on the heavy stuff then, and -- which eventually killed him. So during this time, coming back to the Uptown House, this was something new, you know, because heavy dope at that time was kind of unusual. We, you know, like cocaine and heroin, we really knew nothing about that. We only smoked pot, see.
So it was kind of new, and especially when I came out of the army and I saw all of the musicians using heroin and cocaine I just couldn't understand it.
What relationship, really, do you think it has to music?
Not any as far as I can see.
Why do those musicians, you think, I mean (inaudible).
Well, I'll tell you. You know, it's -- I think it really was an escape, because of the frustrating social conditions, not being able to work here, or certain places you just couldn't work, you know.
Did anybody do you think really feel that it made them more expressive or --
Oh, I don't --
(inaudible) their music. Would anybody want to do it for that reason?
Well, I'll tell you what. There are followers, you know, some people are born followers, and

say like Charlie Parker, it was commonly known that he used dope. So naturally some impressionable young musician assumed that it would make them play better if it worked for Bird -- Bird, it would work for them. Which was not true, you know. So I think this was how it really got kind of out of hand.
But no, I don't think it contributed anything, as a matter of fact.
Do you think they did?
(Inaudible).

Well, sure they did. Sure, I've heard -- I've had -- like Stan Levy told me that Bird -- Bird was like Jezebel. He led everybody, you know. Because not that he consciously tried to do this, but they just were followers, you know. They would do anything he did. You know. So -- but I knew a lot of musicians who were great musicians, didn't touch it. But it's a funny thing, I can tell you -- I hear records that Bird made, and I knew that he was high. And I heard other records that he wasn't high and he played beautifully. But when he was really out of it you could tell it on his record. He wasn't playing as well.
How about smoking pot. Do you think that is a freeing influence in music?
I don't know. No, it didn't help me. For me it was an escape.
From what?
From conditions, social conditions.

Being poor, you know, so I could laugh, you know, and it wouldn't bother me. That was really why I smoked pot. But it came -- once I got to a certain point I just stopped because I realized that it wasn't helping me, you know, it was more or less hindering me. I didn't play as well, you know. I enjoyed playing more but I wasn't playing as well. You know.
And then I think that some people are biologically or chemically stronger than others. I really believe this. Now, there are some guys who probably can handle it. They are --
