Yeah, Lucky Millinder's Blue Rhythm Ribbon something, you know. But he was -- he was almost equally as popular in the same format as Cab Calloway, and Lucky kept -- had a very good band also.
Who was in his band?

Really, I think that Dizzy was in his band at one time, and I can't recall who was in the band, but I know during this same time this was a fad then, you know. The hidey ho and the singing and the dancing of the leaders, you know. So of course Duke was always Duke. He didn't sing nor dance, at that time. He danced in later years, when he got 70.
Yes.
Yes, you know.
Sang a little.
He sang a little, you know. He -- Tell it like it T-I-Z,
A little like (inaudible)
Yeah, he had to wait until he was 70, you know.
What was it like working with Fletcher Henderson's band in Mississippi? You said you couldn't wait to get out of there and didn't want to go back.

Oh, boy, oh, boy. Well, I'll give you an idea. I was in a little town, Rosedale we stopped, and I went into a little place to get a sandwich, so there was an old white man in there, and there was just the two of us. Nobody -- as a matter of fact no one was in there but him, and I went in and I ordered a ham sandwich, and I think a pork sandwich, and he started cutting the meat, slowly, you know. He was very -- I could see him thinking, I could see the wheels turning. This was an old man. So he finally just stuck the knife in the counter, he said, you'll just have to stand outside because this place is too small for white folks and niggers. That gives you an idea of what it was like, you know.

That was a girl vocalist with the group. Her name was Linda something, I don't know, and she liked me, you know. So we played a town called Tupelo, Mississippi, and this girl had to -- she was a very attractive girl, she was a mulatto girl, you know, very light. And she had to send a telegram or something and she wanted me to walk down town with her, so

we -- I've walked, and on our way back there were a car full of white guys and they would drive along and just as we were going to cross the intersection they would stop and park in front of us and we would have to walk around the car. And they were making all kind of remarks, you know.

So this continued every block until we got back where we lived, and when we got to this rooming house the lady who ran the rooming house, she was sitting on the porch and they pulled up in front of there and called her out and told her that they wanted this girl. So she said, well I'll tell you what you do. You come back after the concert tonight and we'll see that, you know --

Well, what had to happen. We left right after the concert, we had to leave town. This is why. We played another town, Vicksburg, Mississippi, and Linda left -- we usually played say the last three numbers without the vocalist, you know, so this night I think she said she had a headache or something and she was going to go home. Well, we lived about two blocks from the auditorium where we were appearing, and after the -- after we finished I went -- we all lived in the same place. I went in, I left the thing, the concert and went home, and as I started to go upstairs in the rooming house this white guy burst out of Linda's room and ran by me, and I recognized the promoter. And he had terrorized this girl, and the land lady. This is what I mean, I was so glad
out of there because you had no -- you know, if you fight back you're dead.

I remember another incident. We were in West Virginia in some little town called Richfield, West Virginia, and we played -- we went -- we got in this town and evidently it was something of a holiday, but we were hungry so we went in this -- we asked someone there, we saw one colored man in this town and we asked him where could we eat, and he said there's a restaurant across the street. He said, that's the only place in town that you can eat. He -- the only -- while he was there he was a bricklayer or something. He was working on a new school they were building. So we went to this restaurant and the owner was very nice, so I sat down, Claude, the trombone player -- what is his name? Claude Jones sat down by me, and Walter Johnson, the drummer. He was right next to me, and the guys were all there.

So in walked about three white guys, and they didn't sit at the counter, because we were at the counter. They sat at a table right behind the counter, right,you know, not behind the counter but behind us. So we got our food and they asked the owner why did he serve these niggers before he served him -- served them, you know.
So he said, in the first place they ordered before you did, but in the interim here comes about six or seven more white guys in while we're talking, so the owner said, well in

the first place they ordered before you did. He said, but -- this white guy said, but these are niggers. This man said, well they're as good as you are. And the fight started between the white guys, you know. They hit the owner, we had to fight our way out of there, you know.

So we finally fight our way, we get out of there, we ran over to the auditorium -- it was an armory, really, but where we were working, and we got in here. So we stayed in here until time to play, and so much harrassment this night, as we were playing. Because the women were pulling at the trombonist's slide as he was sliding, they would dance by and pull at it, you know. So we said, geez, if we can just get out of here soon enough.

So when we finished playing we all packed up and we went downstairs, but we can't leave because they've got Fletcher upstairs playing the piano. They won't let him leave. So finally they let Fletcher get out of there, you know. We got in the bus and we're driving away, and the last thing I heard was these kids who'd been up to the dance hall, goodbye nigger, you know. This is why I was glad to get back, this is -- to New York.
What kind of living -- did you always stay in rooming houses?
Yes.
There were no hotels. No colored hotels?

Well, the hotels -- well, there were some hotels but the hotels were so crummy, you would have fair better if you lived with a family. You know, if you lived with a family or rooming house, you know. Those hotels were---
Rooming houses 2nd boarding houses. (inaudible)
Yeah, the hotels had bed bugs and you know, it was just terrible, you know. So if you could find a nice rooming house or some family even that would take you in, you know.
Did you travel by bus?
We travelled by bus.
You had your own bus. (inaudible)

Yeah, speaking of that, we played a town in Lafayette, Louisiana. Now, Lafayette is south of New Orleans, Opelousas. it's near another little town, Apalusa. It's all around there. And most of the Negroes and white there speak Patois French, you know. So everybody got a room when they got -- before we got there but me, and I was standing out here with my bags and every where and I can't find a rooming house. There's no hotel in the town, and I can't find any place to stay. And everybody is kind of squared away.
So here comes a very attractive creole woman by, and I asked her, Miss, do you have an idea of where I can find a room. We're appearing here tonight and we're going to leave tomorrow.

So she said, well, I have a place, you can come and stay at my place. Fine, so I picked my bags up and followed her to her house, and we went in and it was beautiful inside. The sunken bath tub, the hard wood floors, and all that, you know. Geez, I could hardly believe it.

So fine. I put my bags in the room, beautiful room, and I saw -- I had seen a little bar before I, you know, before I saw her and I was going back to the bar to get a drink. So I went to the bar and a lot of the guys were there, and talking and I was telling them about the fabulous place I was staying in and so on and so on. So after having a few drinks I went back, and when I got there my things were out of the room out on the porch. And I went in and there was a white guy, an old white guy there who would not allow me to stay there. This was his mistress. He -- they put me out.
So you see, these are the reasons I -- you know, that I was so glad to get out of the south. I said Mississippi, but the south period.
Was it a promoter, for instance, would never make any kind of arrangements for living accommodations for a band?
No, they didn't care, no, they didn't -- no --
Well you were on.
You were on your own, yeah. But

usually most of those towns were like a circuit you know, most of the bands, and would play these towns, and most of the guys -- the bus drivers really, who drove us, would know when you got to a town where you could stay, usually. Because they -- You know, like I think Duke had a bus driver for years, and Louie's manager, Frenchy, was our bus driver, with Fletcher.
Frenchy?

Frenchy was our bus driver with Fletcher, as a matter of fact I think Frenchy was with us during these times I'm telling you about. I'm sure Frenchy was, that's where I met Frenchy. Frenchy was our bus driver.
I didn't know that.
Yes. That's right. So they knew all of the stops because they'd gone through here so much with various band, they could tell you right where to stay, where not to go.
Was Frenchy a good friend? Because I heard a lot of people talk about Frenchy bad, they didn't like him.
Well, he was all right as far as I knew but --
During his days with Louis (inaudible) Tyree I think didn't like him. Somebody else.
I don't know. He was all right as far as I was concerned, you know.
He was always nice to me.
Yeah, he was always nice to me. I never had any beefs with him, you know, I couldn't say, you know. Maybe being a manager is a different hing.
He started out being a --
A bus driver, he was a bus driver.
A driver for bands.
That's right, and we went all through the south together. I know this -- that's where I met Frenchy, yes.
You said -- you mentioned at one point that you were living with your God mother whom you said was a very good musician.
Yes.
Who was she?

Her name was Jesse Knight. She was from Montgomery, she was a very fair woman, very -- the red hair, long red hair, and her father was -- reminded me of Santa Claus. He had a flowing white beard, and he was -- well, he was white, you know, really. And when I went to New York I told you I stayed at the Woodside, was my first place to stay. And I got tired of that and I went to live with her.
Did she work professionally for you?
No, she didn't play. She was --
Oh, that's right, you didn't say she was a
Yeah. She played piano.
Did she?

She played very fine piano. But she was like a very -- she was an unusual woman. She was a highly intelligent woman, and she was governess for say like the big, rich families. I mean, a governess. Dietician, you know. And when she was in her late sixties she decided that she wanted to work at the post office, and she took the exams and they never knew -- she was such an agile woman, and such fine physical condition they never knew how old she was. So she worked there until she got out. I think she worked there for years, for six, seven years there. Until she got tired and she quit. This is the type of woman she was. [PAUSE]

Well, now, when I was working with Roy in Chicago, two musicians came from Memphis. One was Tony D'Amico, I believe. He's a pianist, very fine pianist and Mike Bryan, a guitarist. And they used to come to the Three Deuces and see us all the time. When we went to New York they had preceded us, they were already in New York. We went to work on the street, and Mike Bryan was a very fine guitarist. He played in the Van Epps vein. And they had moved -- they had an apartment right up the street from the Kelly's Stables, it was.
And they had this apartment, Mike and Shorty Sherlock

and Sam Rubiwitz, and between sets we would always go up there and we'd smoke a little pot or we'd, you know, and Georgie Auld would be up there every night. And in the meantime Georgie Auld was working with Benny Goodman, and they were looking for a rhythm guitarist, and so I recommended Mike Bryan for the job. Because Georgie used to come down and blow with us every night at Kelly's Stables, you know.

And Mike made the audition and got the job. In the meantime Charlie Christian was the featured guitarist, and consequently Mike and Charlie became very good friends, and Charlie Christian gave Mike an electric guitar, and an amplifier, that Gibson had given him. But they were giving Charlie quite a few guitars at that time so he gave him a new guitar and amplifier and Charlie gave it to Mike. And Mike out of appreciation for my getting him the job gave me the electric -- Charlie's electric guitar and amplifier. This was the first electric guitar I ever had.

And I would try to play it on the stand with Roy, and Roy didn't like the sound of the electric guitar, and we would fight every night because Roy wanted me to play acoustic guitar. But the mere fact that it was Charlie's guitar I was going to fight Roy. But that's really how I started playing electric guitar. And my first electric guitar was Charlie Christian's guitar. So I thought there would be of interest.
Incidently, Mike Bryan worked with Benny for quite a

while, and he just died not too long ago here in Los Angeles. But he also was producing a show in Europe for the Ford Foundation. Some kind of jazz show over there. And he would bring all the big musicians from here, from America over there to do these shows. Mike was quite a guy.

But any way he died about a year ago, and Georgia All came by to tell me because we were all very dear friends. Now, I had to just inject that because I didn't -- I thought it would be of some interest to you. [PAUSE]
Somewhere back, I think on our second tape, you mentioned a white singer who sang like Billy Eckstein, but you couldn't remember his last name.
You've remembered (Inaudible).
Yeah, it was Bill Farrow. And he made this tune, it really made him famous. I mentioned it before, what was it -- well, okay.
I guess it's on tape number two. (Inaudible).

Yeah, but any way he later did quite a few things with Bob Hope. Bob Hope had this television show with Les Brown's band, and Bill Farrow was the featured vocalist on there. Very fine singer though, you know, But in thinking about Benny Carter, I don't know whether I mentioned before that I did quite a few recordings with Benny. This for Bob Freedman. This is a guy from Florida who was a song writer, and he wrote so many tunes, and he wanted to hear them all on records, so he wanted them all

recorded, and he wanted Benny to do them. And so Benny assembled the musicians and he had just about everybody that was anybody in Los Angeles on this day. And Bob Freedman brought Flip Phillips from Florida with him to do these recordings. And it was just nice seeing Flip after so many years and it was -- we were doing these tapes during the Christmas season, and on one -- tapes, this album, rather.
Several albums.

Yeah, but this particular date Flip brought me a Christmas present, and it was a picture, an old picture of Les Young, Prez and myself, playing, just the two of us. And it was just the greatest thing he could have done. He said, well John, I knew you were going to be on the date so I brought this from Florida just to give you because I knew you'd like to have it. And I have it. I had it framed, it's just a marvelous thing.

But I think I told you I did some other -- I've done so many things with Benny recently. I did a movie, as a matter of fact I saw the movie last night, and -- of Sidney Potier and Harry Belafonte, 'Buck and the Preacher.' Benny wrote the whole score for this movie and they threw it out. The Poitier and Belafonte didn't want it. They wanted -- well it was a good score but they wanted something more earthy. They had -- so they got about six or seven guitars, some harmonicas, and drums and let's see, and what do you call it,
the mouth organ, the juice harp, or whatever they call the mouth organ. And it really came off good though, and everything was just spontaneous. As we saw the movie we would play, and --
Sort of scored it yourself. (Inaudible).
Yeah, just right on the spot. You know, it came off beautifully --
Totally improvised score.

Yeah, that's right, that's right. And it came off beautifully. And I'm trying to think of the guitarist. It was Howard Roberts, Al Viola, and let's see who else. Me of course, and one other guitarist, and Donald Bailey was playing drums and mouth organ.
Oh.

Yeah, he plays very good mouth organ. And they had another guy by the name of Tommy Morgan, Tom Morgan. But any way it was just nice to see it because I had never seen the movie and it was on television last night, and it occurred to me how this whole background, musical background occurred. It was just a spontaneous thing.

And after that I went to New York, Philadelphia, Baltimore -- not Baltimore, Boston, and Washington with Benny, accompanying a singer, Marie Muldas. In the band was Harry Edison Addison, Marty Harris playing piano, John Williams playing bass, Earl --
Palmer?

-- Palmer drums, Plas Johnson, saxophone. And Frank Assolino, Snooky Young. But I don't think that Maria Muldar realized what -- how good the band was, you know. So consequently we got the write ups. The people, the critics would come to see her and we would get the write ups. If -- they loved her, but, you know, the band-- we had a couple of featured numbers, and that was it. You know. But she's so sweet she enjoyed it all and it just knocked her out. But I think that if she had known she would have given the band billing, you know.

But any way, I want to say this about Maria Muldar. The one thing that impressed me, the first time I heard her sing -- as a matter of fact we did an album with her. This -- so we did this tour as a result of the album. But the one thing that impressed me about Maria Muldar, she sounded like Mildred Bailey. And I asked her had she ever heard Mildred at this time and she said, no, but several people had told her this. But she sounded like, just like Mildred Bailey, a young Mildred Bailey.

So, you know, she -- I took her right to my heart there, as soon as I heard that. I think she was special to all of us then, you know, and she felt it. But we had a very successful tour with Lady Muldar.
That album you did, is that Wafers in

I think so, yes, yes. But you know, she's a very astute young lady. I -- we did one thing, one tune we did, transbluency. Now, this was done by Duke and Kay Davis. No lyrics, just voice and horns. So I -- it came off so well, Maria -- Marie -- Benny Carter was playing the horn, you know, so it was just like a duet. And I -- and of course Benny arranged it for her. And I said, Benny, that was a marvelous idea you had for Maria Muldaur. He said, no, John, she heard this record and had the idea and approached me about it.
(Inaudible)
She heard Kay and Duke's record?

She heard the record and she approached -- Benny, she said, I'd like to do that, he said I can't take credit for that. You know, despite the fact that it came off so beautifully he said it was her idea, not mine. And she did quite a few of Duke's things and some of Billie Holiday's things. But she lives in Woodstock so you know where her roots are. She's really -- how would you say, a folk singer? From that school, any way. You know. But she's -- I think she's going places in the contemporary you know, in the jazz world I think that she'll make it. Very good.
I've read several reviews of hers, and they made reference to Kay's record, and I told Kay when
Yeah.
--and she said I didn't think anybody remembered me any more.
Oh, boy, how can they forget her. Yeah, but any way it was Maria's idea, it was not Benny's. So I wasn't aware of that. But a very successful tour.

You were talking about the personnel of Fletcher Henderson's band when you were in it, and you got as far as Joe Keys, Pops Smith, Jonah Jones, trumpet, and you mentioned Clyde Jones, Sandy Williams on trombone. And then later you mentioned Walter Johnson on drums. Who else can you remember?

Well, now, George Irish, a very fine tenor player from Boston, who's with us. Freddy Mitchell, who's another very good tenor player from New York, and Rudy Powell, alto. Everybody knows Rudy. He was with everybody. He was with Teddy Wilson's band, a very good band, when Ben was there, and J. C. And George Dorsey was alto, and Ted Sturges a bass Bates, and I don't know how I could have forgot Peanuts Holland. He was playing trumpet then, a very fine trumpet player. He was one of the giants, you know.
So that was -- most of the band that I can remember at this point.
We also talked about the -- Frank Sinatra, and I know you worked with him in live performance.
Have you ever recorded with Frank?

No, I never recorded with Frank. I only did -- well, you know, I worked with him in Vegas quite a bit, and I did some tours with him, you know, but I just never recorded with him. Actually Al Viola was his guitarist, Al has been recording with him and working with him for years and years. But I would replace Al when Al couldn't make it or something, I would replace him. And it was quite a pleasure working with Frank because he's got that charisma, and he is quite a musician also. You know, he's just a perfectionist and it's a pleasure, it was a pleasure to be associated with him, to work with him. Because he carried the best musicians with him too, and so it was a pleasure working with them.

You know, he carried his own key men. Of course Bill Miller, as I mentioned, was playing piano for Red Norro and Mildred Bailey when I first met him in the thirties. He's been Frank's conductor for quite a few years, and Pete Condola was the first trumpet player, and the drummer -- Irv Cotler.
Irv Cotler.

Irv Cotler, and he had two violinists, Raderman, Mrs. Raderman, I can't think of their -- Sally Raderman and Lou Raderman. And he didn't have a bass with us, we would pick up a bass when we -- when I was with him, and myself. And I would always -- he's alway featuring me, and I would always do a number with him. I would take --
we would get the stool and we would do the bit together, and that was a thrill because I just loved playing for him, you know.
Didn't like his politics, of course, but --
You mean his latter day politics.
Yes, that's right.
His earlier politics were all right
(inaudible)
Yeah, they were all right, but, you know, he's like a chameleon, he just changes colors on those politics, you know.

You mentioned very briefly the all night sessions you used to have in the New York with Tal Roney Farlow and Jimmy Rannie and Sal Salvador, talking and playing all night long. Did you find those kind of sessions just with eachother more stimulating and productive than had you been playing for audiences?

Oh, naturally, because we could do it over, you know. And we exchanged ideas, and it was just the-- you know, it wasn't a frantic thing where we just played. We played until we, you know, got tired and we'd stop, we'd talk, have coffee, or something, just play. It was just good fellowship, you know, and that was quite enjoyable. Yeah, I enjoyed it.
But then I wanted -- did I mention the thing that I did with Benny and Bob Freeman? I did mention that, didn't
I? Yeah, but that was the -- personnel of that band -- I can't remember all of it but it was just a beautiful band.
I remember it, yeah.
That's right, you were there. And Carmen McRae sang some of the tunes and --
And Joe Williams sang.

Joe Williams sang some, and another girl, Ernestine Anderson, who I love. She sang some. I wonder what ever happened to her. She's a marvelous singer. I think she went back to Seattle. I hired her for a few jobs after that. I had -- casuals and I would always call her, because I enjoyed her singing so much.

Those were fabulous days (inaudible) Bob Freedman (maybe we should differentiate him from many other Bob Freedmans. This is the Bob Freedman who had no prior music reputation. He was a retired manufacturer --
Manufacturer, yeah.
-- who always wanted to be a song writer, and made enough money in bolt manufacturing or some kind of (metal) manufacturing.
Yeah, in Florida.
So that he could indulge himself. So he wrote songs and hired an absolute dream band.
That's right.
Was Benny doing all the (inaudible) and with arrangements
Yeah. Ray Brown was bass. Who played drums? Shelly Manne?
Shelly Manne and --
And Louie Bellson.
Bellson and Paul Humphreys.
Paul Humphreys, yeah, that's right, that's right. And the two guitarists, me and Barney Kessel. And Jimmy Jones, pianist, and --
It's like a Who's Who of Hollywood musicians.
That's right, it was just -- yeah, it was a beautiful, beautiful thing.
Did you ever get to know Paul Robeson at all on all those dates you played with him or --

Well, I didn't get to know him then, because I couldn't get to him for the people. But in later years he moved into my -- I lived in a -- let's see, how do I say it, the metropolitan development. It's like apartments -- it's called the Riverton in New York, 135th and Madison. And he also lived in this development. I got to know him then. Beautiful man, just a marvelous, marvelous human being. And I realized that this man sacrificed his whole career for --
(Tape 8)
We were talking about Paul Robeson.

Yeah, I realized in later years that this man sacrificed his whole career to make the white man aware of the Negro. Because Paul Robeson at this time was -- he was a brilliant actor, a brilliant singer, he was a Rhodes scholar, he was an all American football player, he was just everything. And he just killed himself, you know, his career. But in doing so he made the white man aware of the fact that he had to reckon with the black man. He just couldn't take him as Sambo, you know. He -- Jackie Robinson, I remember when he -- he didn't understand Paul Robeson at first. He -- but he finally came around and recognized the fact that Paul Robeson was a great man in what he had done for his people.
And I would catch him out in the court every now and then in Riverton and just talk to him, and it was just the man had a beautiful philosophy, he was a beautiful human being.
He was very, very interested in all kinds of music.
That's right, that's right.
He loved jazz and --
Yes.
-- and he had done a lot of studying because he believed that in the possibility that some of the roots of jazz were -- roots of European music were African.
Yes.
He found similarities in European clas-
sical music --
Yes, yes.
-- American jazz, and I had think it's a fascinating -- conversation with him once,

Here we go again. I was talking about young musicians, and the extension of what had been done before by the older generation of music. But the young musician should study the history of black jazz, black music. This is particularly. And really get into it because it's quite interesting. It's very informative, as a matter of fact. They really should study this and it's -- it will amaze them what the black musician has, you know, the African from Africa on has contributed as far as music is concerned. [PAUSE]
Did you feel any special musical kinship with Lester Young? You said that Lester liked your beat and that you always found eachother at jam sessions. What was your musical relationship?

Well, naturally we had a musical rapport. We just dug eachother. And when he would come to Chicago with Basie he would always find me, I'd find him, we'd find eachother, and we would play together every night. We used to go around to clubs and find places to play. One place we used to go to in particular was on 51st Street, and why I mention this is Israel Crosby's sister, siste worked in this club. One played drums and one played piano. And we would
go over and just take over the job and jam all night long, you know.

So they would always try to get me to come to New York, you know, to -- so finally when I did go there we just got together right away. You know, as a matter of fact he had just left Basie, and we just took up where we left off in Chicago. And we played every day. We would go downstairs in the hotel, in the Woodside Hotel, and play every day, as I told you, without piano. We would just have piano -- I mean guitar, bass, drums, Prez, and Shad Collins, and finally Betty Roche started dropping in and so she became our vocalist. She would sing with us every day. She was there every day. And finally I mean, eventually I brought Clyde in.
Clyde who?

Clyde Hart. I asked Clyde, because I used to play checkers with Clyde every night. Me, John Williams who was Mary Lou Williams' husband, and Joe Jones who thought he could play checkers. And this was every night. So I prevailed upon Clyde to come by rehearsal, and he played and eventually he just started working with us. You know, but Lester, yes. This is why I told you when I saw him after the war, I detected right away that something had happened to him. I could see it right away, because I knew him so well.
He wasn't the same, you know. Something had -- he
looked like he was burned out. You know, he was playing -- you had to know him well to tell this, but I knew this. That something had happened.
So any way we did have a very -- we had a kinship, we were very close. Which I can't say for his brother and I, but --
Well you worked together for a long time
(Inaudible).
Well, we worked together for a long time, but Lee was a fine drummer, fine musician. But they were -- it's a funny thing. He and Lester were alike in a lot of ways and in many ways they weren't.
is he not?
Well Lee was more outgoing (inaudible).
Not really.
He's always seemed like it to me.
Really? (inaudible).
Yeah, but Lee is -- how can I put this -- Lee likes to be at the right place at the right time. Okay.
He knows
Yes. You've got to take advantage of (inaudible) when he's there. He's a businessman.

Yeah. And if he's not -- that's right, and if he's not in the right place he'll leave right away, you know. Okay? So there's a difference, you know. But Prez was just all music. Music was the thing, you know. And that was it, and with Lee it was a little more business attached to it than with Prez.
I see some more notes of yours. What

have you got written down there? Well, I want to mention the fact that I did work with Neal Hefti quite a bit this past summer. He had a band, he formed another band. He got the yen to conduct again, and that was quite a pleasure. We worked Disney band and quite a few casuals, and Nat Pierce was the pianist. And Frankie Capp was drummer, and it was a very good band, any way. And I did quite a bit of recording with Billy May. Now, the -- here we go again.
You don't remember.
I don't remember what they were, you know. But I also --
Do you know what label? Capitol?

It was Capitol, yeah, yeah. I also want to go back to Detroit, we were talking about Gerald Wilson (up there) when we picked him didn't we. And at this time I met a pianist who played so much like Art Tatum, his name was Willie Hawkins. And he finally came out here but he got ill and he went back to Detroit, and I think he died. And this is where I met Al McKibbon, during that same time, and we got Gerald Wilson out of there.
Al McKibbons.
Al McKibbons from Detroit, and I met another very fine drummer at that time, Kelly Martin. He was a drummer with Errol in later years. Very fine drummer. But

I want to say Willie Hawkins, these are the two guys that really sounded to me like Art, was Willie Hawkins and it was another guy in Cleveland, from Cleveland rather. Lanny Scott. Did I mention Lanny, that I saw him playing with Jonah's band in Boston this past season, with Cozy Cole and John Brown playing bass. But I just heard that Lanny just died also. But he was one of the few guys that really sounded like Art. You know, well he's from Cleveland too, and Art was just his idol.
So I think that about wraps it up.
Thank you very much.
(End of proceedings as recorded.)
SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION

Interview with John Birks Gillespie
(About John Collins) by Patricia Willard

Washington, D. C.
March 29, 1975

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.
PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE
AREA CODE 202 347-5395
PROCEEDINGS
What do you want me to say about John?

Whatever you want to say about John but last year I believe it was I gave you the name when you were being interviewed and you made a statement about John and what he gave you musically or what you had learned from his musically; an evaluation that was something I'd never heard before. So what I would like to know is that statement and then your evaluation of John.

Well, before that time I'd never been closely associated with any guitar player. Well before I met John I hadn't been closely associated with any guitar players, you know, with the exception of -- well before I met Charley Christian I met John Collins and John Collins was always the studious one. He was always figuring out different variations and changes.

He'd say, 'Hey, look here', cause I played the piano and he'd say, 'Look at this'. He always had some different way of doing things. You know like most of the guys when they played, 'Man I Loved', this particular part most of the guys played B flat. John maybe did B flat minus six chords, things like that that really opened my eyes because actually John was more advanced musically than I was.

He was older than I and he'd been in heavier company than I had been in and so, therefore, from my experience with John I learned a lot because he had been in the company of bigger guys than I had been. We were all -- you see, the company that I was in was Johnny Clark, Monk, Bud Powers wasn't there yet; he was a young, young kid and hadn't come on the scene yet, and Scottie and all these guys, Ben Harris, Charlie Shavers.
Well, John Collins was a step above us and he used to help.
In what year was this that you met John?
Well it must have been like 1937.
And didn't he subsequently work with you?

Well, he made records with me and we worked together in 1942 with Benny Carter and that was a great experience too because we had two -- three of the foremost exponents of the instrument like -- three. There was Benny Carter, there was Kenny Clark, there was John and then there was Sonny White, and that was a great experience for me too because well at that time I was getting a little name and I was getting a new dialogue, you know, setting up notes together. That was a big experience with Benny Carter, John Collins, Kenny Clark and Sonny White. It was a great

band too.
John was really one of the major voices on the guitar. Before Charley Christian came, John was the guitar player, the guitar player, you know. Of course when Charley Christian came on the scene, Charley Christian had a far western outlook to music, you know, like Oklahoma. So he had that thing and that really set his apart from the rest of the musicians and then he came into jamming with us. So John was really a major voice.
You said there were a lot of important musical lessons as I recall that you learned from him in the advanced harmonics?
Yes.
Things that he was playing then that you had not heard before?
Yes.
Thank you.

You see, what John knows and what he does there are no books, there are no books that will show you what he does because that guy has been practicing for the last -- oh man, he's been practicing every since I've been knowing him and see I've been knowing him since the early '40s, and he puts in time on that instrument.
See, he makes things on that guitar that nobody --

progressions and voice. You know, a lot of guys make the same progression, you know, progression like going from E minor to A 7 flat or with an added 11 and this that John, nobody is as sophisticated as he is and nobody has been that sophisticated.

You see, this guy -- that guitar now is like -- well like he's got three hands now. He's got one picking the guitar, he's got one fingering and the guitar is another hand. He's three handed, this motherfucker.

The other day he came by -- came by where I spent the night, the other night when he was behind us and he came by over there and so we had a little aside and I was telling him about my religious faith and everything --
(Recording Interruption)

-- and see this guy plays with Jimmy Smith -- was playing, he was playing for hours back in the back room there. John took that guitar and came up in the living room and this is where he and I were sitting there. Boy, this is -- the way that he plays, his voicing on there is like a harp.

It's like he's playing a harp only he's faster than a harp, you know, and the way -- you should -- I was looking at the way his fingers were stretched out. This guy plays some hard shit on that guitar. I mean, it is not easy what he's doing. It is not easy. It takes practice, practice, practice, practice and some more practice for what he does on
the guitar and he's been like that ever since I've been knowing him.

You know, I know a lot of the things that he does, the progressions because he was always -- he recognized the fact that I was sophisticated with progressions. I taught Miles progressions, Tad, showed Monk a lot of things and -- now don't -- I'm not saying that I didn't learn from all of them, you know what I mean, but I showed -- you see, I was always a piano player and I told him the other day, "Man, I always wanted to play a guitar". He said, "Nigger, you play enough piano". He said, "You should have been playing the guitar", because I would do the same thing, you see.

If I was playing the guitar, I'd be playing like John Collins because when I make an arrangement there is no set -- you know, like guys -- like Quincy and those guys have set things that they put in the arrangement. Now they just put that down by arrangement, you know, but me, I feel out every note, every chord, everything, you know.

The voicing, I figure out the voicing because I don't know how it's going to sound before. An arrangement on the piano, what sounds good on the piano doesn't sound good with instruments. So I have to make adjustments all the time. That's why I don't write because it takes me months to make an arrangement, a couple of months maybe to get it like I want it, you know.

I'll be scratching shit, you know, but that John Collins, I told him, I said, "Hey man," I said, "You know what you should do. You should make an album just with yourself because ain't nobody -- ain't no bass player could do it with you with the possible exception of Ray Brown that I know that's living now that would do a good job", with what John knows.
He would have to spend his time explaining. Ray has got some ears too. See John has got the ears. He's a bad cat.
(Inaudible).
Huh?
He has never recorded a solo album or he has never recorded as a leader.
No, I know it.
I didn't realize that.
As a matter of fact, when I see Norman Grant, I'm going to tell Norman Grant that I want John Collins, that's true.
He's the greatest.

Since I've made one with Oscar -- I came out here and spent a week with him and we woodshedded -- just playing -- woodshed -- and stuck our heads together and make an album. It would be a hell of an album.
It sure would.
It would be a hell of an album because ain't nobody --
(Recording Interruption)
-- and the voicing that goes with it.
When -- Leonard __________, he said that John was one of the Charley Christian inspired guitarists but then you said that John was the prime influence --
Uh-uh.
-- in New York up until the time --

Yeah. You see, let me show you the difference in the plane. Christian wasn't as deep as John. You see, Christian was a blockbuster, you know. That area that he came from produced that -- guys that played like that, one note. He'd take one note and run you crazy, you know, Charley Christian, and Charley Christian recognized the talents of John Collins.

He recognized it. He knew he was bad, you know, and we used to talk about him. We used to talk about John Collins with Charley Christian. "What do you think of John Collins". He'd say, "Whew", because I'm telling you --
Did Christian learn from John?

No, he was in another -- another -- I imagine -- I imagine he did, you know, because John was a master progressionist -- you know progressionist -- going from here to here to here to here to here to here. Christian was a

-- let's see, how would you call that -- well he -- Christian was the first one that was heard because he was the first one to play electric guitar. The rest of the guys -- John used to play -- he'd be playing and rhythm, you should hear him play rhythm. Every chord -- you see, every stroke he makes is a different change. He don't say, "bang, bang, bang, bang", he says, "dom ding dum dum ding dum", you know what I mean?

He'll play, you know, he don't make one chord. You know, like you're in a bar, if you've got one chord in a bar now he's progressing all the time. It's a joy to play with a guy like that, really. I don't know nobody that I'd rather play with than him.
(Inaudible).
I really don't.
I really dig him, yeah.
I really don't. He's a bad cat. I recognize his talent -- a long time. Shoot, we're out here ain't we?
Yeah.
What time is the flight?
Shoot, we've got 35 minutes. Find the musicians and let them know that I'm going to make it.
(End of proceedings as recorded.)

MS. WILLARD: Conversation with Benny Carter about John Collins.

Yes.
In New York.
Yes. He said, 'They think "Super Sax" is such a big deal', he said, 'Benny did that on that album with Coleman Hawkins'.
Oh, well I didn't do much on that but he did do that. That's right. You don't have those albums, do you?
I don't have them, no.
I have them for you if you want them.
Oh, I'd love to have them.
Oh sure. Both of them I have for you.
Wonderful, wonderful, and then do you remember the times he recorded with you before in New York, --
No, I don't.
-- way back, because he says he knows he recorded with you but he can't remember what or when or whom?
I can't either, but he did that album with me with Ella Fitzgerald, 'Thirty by Ella'. I don't even

Yeah, he mentioned that one.
Three or four years at Capitol.
Um hmmm.
I'm very foggy about that. You know, John is really one of my favorite guitarists. A lot of people say he's underrated but he's not underrated. He's just not rated by people who don't know him.
Yeah, he was --
You know, we that know him really don't underrate him, you know.

Yeah, that's what I was telling him because I had this big stack of jazz books here while we were talking and he went through them as I had done and he's not in any of them. All he's in is Leonard's Encyclopedia and the Who's Who of Jazz by Chilton.

That's right.
-- but he's never had any kind of public acclaim, he's never been written about, the critics ignore him and --

Well, I don't -- I don't know how to, you know, state that, you know. I would certainly say he is -- he should enjoy a very, very important place.
