segments.chapter: Childhood and first guitar
segments.title: Copyright notice, title page and start of interview
segments.summary: Copyright warnings and title page for the 1975 Smithsonian interview with John Collins by Patricia Willard; Willard proposes going chronologically from Montgomery.

segments.chapter: Childhood and first guitar
segments.title: Mother, grandmother and W. C. Handy in Montgomery
segments.summary: Collins says his mother and grandmother were fine pianists who taught music, and his mother demonstrated sheet music for W. C. Handy with Fletcher Henderson. They tried to discourage him from playing piano.

segments.chapter: Childhood and first guitar
segments.title: Playing in his mother's band as a boy
segments.summary: From about age twelve he played in his mother's band alongside pros like Lorenzo Wardell and Alton Moore, and Handy's band would visit the house.

segments.chapter: Childhood and first guitar
segments.title: Teaching himself guitar after hearing Eddie Lang
segments.summary: Hearing Eddie Lang made him decide to be a guitarist; he taught himself unorthodox voicings over years.

segments.chapter: Childhood and first guitar
segments.title: Moving to Chicago; school with Ray Nance
segments.summary: The family moved to Chicago in the 1920s; at Wendell Phillips High School he played in Ray Nance's band.

segments.chapter: Childhood and first guitar
segments.title: House rent parties during the Depression
segments.summary: He and his mother played the rent-party circuit with Dan Grissom, and they were paid.

segments.chapter: Childhood and first guitar
segments.title: His mother as pianist and taskmaster
segments.summary: Collins credits his mother's immaculate taste and strictness; she led a trio and did rehearsal work at the Oriental and Chicago Theatres.

segments.chapter: Childhood and first guitar
segments.title: Post office job and meeting John Levy
segments.summary: His father pushed him into a special delivery job at the post office at about sixteen, where he met pianist John Levy.

segments.chapter: Childhood and first guitar
segments.title: From ukulele and banjo to guitar; no teachers; hearing counterpoint in church
segments.summary: He started on his sister's ukulele, moved to banjo and guitar, had no teacher available, and developed his own voicings, helped by hearing counterpoint at his mother's choir rehearsals.

segments.chapter: Childhood and first guitar
segments.title: Charlie Christian, Minton's and the Leonard Feather label
segments.summary: Collins insists he never tried to play like Charlie Christian, recalls hearing him at Minton's and meeting him at Monroe's Uptown House, and objects to being labeled Christian-inspired.

segments.chapter: Chicago: Henderson, Tatum and Roy Eldridge, then New York and the army
segments.title: Auditioning for Fletcher Henderson without saying who he was
segments.summary: After his mother's death he moved to New York in 1940 and won the Henderson guitar job without revealing that Henderson knew his mother, telling him six months later on a bus in Mississippi.

segments.chapter: Chicago: Henderson, Tatum and Roy Eldridge, then New York and the army
segments.title: Two years with Art Tatum at the Three Deuces
segments.summary: Collins worked nightly with Tatum in Chicago, made his first recorded solo, absorbed Tatum's voicings, and went to after-hours spots where Tatum introduced him to Billie Holiday.

segments.chapter: Chicago: Henderson, Tatum and Roy Eldridge, then New York and the army
segments.title: Forming and playing in Roy Eldridge's band at the Three Deuces
segments.summary: After Eldridge left Henderson he formed a small band in Chicago with Collins, Dave Young, Scoops Carey, Zutty Singleton and Truck Parham, staying about three years.

segments.chapter: Chicago: Henderson, Tatum and Roy Eldridge, then New York and the army
segments.title: Segregation in Chicago clubs and restaurants
segments.summary: The Three Deuces took only white patrons and Chicago was prejudiced about restaurants and hotels, which Collins says changed during World War II.

segments.chapter: Chicago: Henderson, Tatum and Roy Eldridge, then New York and the army
segments.title: Jam sessions at the Three Deuces: Waller, Basie's band, Lester Young
segments.summary: Touring bands came to the club, Fats Waller brought his band to jam, and Basie's band, on their first trip out of Kansas City, jammed all night with Lester Young and Ben Webster.

segments.chapter: Chicago: Henderson, Tatum and Roy Eldridge, then New York and the army
segments.title: Savoy Ballroom with Roy Eldridge and meeting Dizzy Gillespie
segments.summary: Collins first went to New York with Eldridge, who played opposite Erskine Hawkins, and he noticed Dizzy Gillespie, harmonically different from anyone, jamming with Roy.

segments.chapter: Chicago: Henderson, Tatum and Roy Eldridge, then New York and the army
segments.title: Charlie Parker as 'the Shadow' who sold pot
segments.summary: In New York around 1940 Collins knew Parker only as a pot seller in a dark coat, until Parker sat in at an Eldridge rehearsal and stunned him.

segments.chapter: Chicago: Henderson, Tatum and Roy Eldridge, then New York and the army
segments.title: Dizzy as a true original; jamming with Dizzy and Ben Webster
segments.summary: Dizzy was different from other Eldridge imitators; they jammed in Collins's hotel room and at the Grampion Hotel with Ben Webster.

segments.chapter: Chicago: Henderson, Tatum and Roy Eldridge, then New York and the army
segments.title: Replacing Willie Lewis in Benny Carter's band after Henderson
segments.summary: Tired of the road with Henderson, Collins visited Kelly's Stables, heard Nat Cole and Benny Carter, and accepted Carter's offer to stay.

segments.chapter: Chicago: Henderson, Tatum and Roy Eldridge, then New York and the army
segments.title: Carter's Kelly's Stables bill; the draft notice and Carter's appeal
segments.summary: The Kelly's show with Carter, Nat Cole's trio, Tatum and Miss Rhapsody; later at the Apollo Collins was drafted and Carter appeared with him before the board.

segments.chapter: Chicago: Henderson, Tatum and Roy Eldridge, then New York and the army
segments.title: Teaching Tiny Grimes for Tatum while in the army
segments.summary: On furlough in 1942 Collins taught Tiny Grimes chords and voicings for Tatum's trio, and says four army years kept him off the scene.

segments.chapter: Chicago: Henderson, Tatum and Roy Eldridge, then New York and the army
segments.title: Guitarists before Charlie Christian
segments.summary: Floyd Smith got a little attention, but Christian's electric guitar made people aware of the instrument.

segments.chapter: Chicago: Henderson, Tatum and Roy Eldridge, then New York and the army
segments.title: Roy Eldridge at the Arcadia and Kelly's Stables
segments.summary: Collins worked in Eldridge's big band and small group; at Kelly's Stables he met Leonard Feather and saw the Harlem Highlanders and the pimps and hustlers.

segments.chapter: Chicago: Henderson, Tatum and Roy Eldridge, then New York and the army
segments.title: Getting Charlie Christian's electric guitar through Mike Bryan; Eddie Durham
segments.summary: He recommended Mike Bryan for Benny Goodman's band, and Bryan gave him Christian's guitar and amplifier, his first electric; he notes Eddie Durham amplified guitar before Christian.

segments.chapter: Chicago: Henderson, Tatum and Roy Eldridge, then New York and the army
segments.title: Using the army years to practice
segments.summary: In the army he practiced and compared what he heard on New York trips, returning in 1946 to a changed bebop scene.

segments.chapter: Bebop, Tadd Dameron, Slam Stewart and Europe
segments.title: Tadd Dameron, bass lines and the Woodside Hotel
segments.summary: Collins corrected Tadd Dameron's bass lines before the war, and on his return Dameron repaid him by showing him bebop on an organ.

segments.chapter: Bebop, Tadd Dameron, Slam Stewart and Europe
segments.title: How music changed with bebop; meeting Sarah Vaughan
segments.summary: Postwar music had fast, changing tempos and was for listening, not dancing; Collins felt at home, and Dameron introduced him to Sarah Vaughan.

segments.chapter: Bebop, Tadd Dameron, Slam Stewart and Europe
segments.title: Freddy Webster and Dameron in Cleveland circles
segments.summary: Trumpeter Freddy Webster played for Collins and his godmother, and the three hung out together.

segments.chapter: Bebop, Tadd Dameron, Slam Stewart and Europe
segments.title: Slam Stewart trio, Billy Taylor and Beryl Booker
segments.summary: After the army Collins joined Slam Stewart's group with Billy Taylor; Taylor was fired after his honeymoon and replaced by Beryl Booker.

segments.chapter: Bebop, Tadd Dameron, Slam Stewart and Europe
segments.title: Beryl Booker playing an arrangement in B natural
segments.summary: Collins tells how a tipsy Beryl Booker played a rehearsed tune a half step off, perfectly, in B natural.

segments.chapter: Bebop, Tadd Dameron, Slam Stewart and Europe
segments.title: Europe in 1947 with Slam Stewart and Erroll Garner
segments.summary: The trio went to Paris with Coleman Hawkins, Howard McGhee and blues singer Chippie Hill; Garner had won a poll, and Collins met Nicole Barclay.

segments.chapter: Bebop, Tadd Dameron, Slam Stewart and Europe
segments.title: Erroll Garner in Pittsburgh and Jimmy Blanton
segments.summary: Collins recalls first seeing Garner at a Pittsburgh club wiping his brow every eight bars, and seeing Jimmy Blanton on a riverboat.

segments.chapter: Bebop, Tadd Dameron, Slam Stewart and Europe
segments.title: Linton Garner and Erroll's European poll
segments.summary: Collins met Erroll's brother Linton during a big show with Nat and Duke, and confirms Garner's poll win rested on his Slam Stewart recordings and the Paris engagement lasted three weeks.

segments.chapter: Bebop, Tadd Dameron, Slam Stewart and Europe
segments.title: Leaving Slam Stewart and laying off
segments.summary: Slam and Beryl drank and Collins tired of managing them, so he quit and stopped playing professionally for a while.

segments.chapter: Royal Roost, Birdland and Three O'Clock High
segments.title: Sorting out Bop City, Royal Roost and Birdland dates
segments.summary: Collins and Willard work out the order in which Bop City, Birdland and the Royal Roost opened.

segments.chapter: Royal Roost, Birdland and Three O'Clock High
segments.title: Tadd Dameron's band with guitar lead; 'Focus' and 'John's Delight'
segments.summary: Dameron wrote guitar lead parts for Collins; the recordings, including 'Focus' and Collins's 'John's Delight,' won a record of the year award.

segments.chapter: Royal Roost, Birdland and Three O'Clock High
segments.title: Royal Roost: drugs, the band and Miles Davis sitting in
segments.summary: Collins describes the junkie culture at the Royal Roost, the dealer who sat with the band, and Miles Davis playing nightly without pay.

segments.chapter: Royal Roost, Birdland and Three O'Clock High
segments.title: Dameron's bad check and the Kay Penton records
segments.summary: Dameron paid the band out of pocket and gave Collins a check on a nearly empty account; they recorded with singer Kay Penton.

segments.chapter: Royal Roost, Birdland and Three O'Clock High
segments.title: Harry Belafonte as house singer at the Royal Roost
segments.summary: Belafonte then sang like Billy Eckstine and the guys put him down; later he told Collins on Nat Cole's show that he had made it.

segments.chapter: Royal Roost, Birdland and Three O'Clock High
segments.title: Addiction among Royal Roost players and back with Slam at Bop City
segments.summary: Collins names J. J. Johnson as having beaten heroin, then rejoined Slam Stewart at Bop City.

segments.chapter: Royal Roost, Birdland and Three O'Clock High
segments.title: Elliot Lawrence's band opposite them
segments.summary: Elliot Lawrence's band with Gerry Mulligan and a Eckstine-style white singer played opposite them at Bop City.

segments.chapter: Royal Roost, Birdland and Three O'Clock High
segments.title: House quartet at Birdland with Billy Taylor; Sarah Vaughan
segments.summary: Collins was in the Birdland house group with Billy Taylor, Al McKibbon and Jo Jones, and first worked with Sarah Vaughan there.

segments.chapter: Royal Roost, Birdland and Three O'Clock High
segments.title: Three O'Clock High: booking Sunday concerts without agents
segments.summary: With Art Blakey he formed a company that booked stars directly for Sunday concerts, mostly losing money.

segments.chapter: Royal Roost, Birdland and Three O'Clock High
segments.title: Miles Davis and the Audubon Ballroom Sundays
segments.summary: Collins brought Miles to play a Sunday and was accused of cheating him; the concerts at the Audubon paid scale and Collins watched the money.

segments.chapter: Fourteen years with Nat Cole and the recording sessions
segments.title: Leaving Tatum to join Nat Cole
segments.summary: Collins worked again with Tatum, then Nat Cole called; Tatum reluctantly let him go and he stayed about fourteen years until Cole died.

segments.chapter: Fourteen years with Nat Cole and the recording sessions
segments.title: The trio becomes a singing act: Marie's idea
segments.summary: At the Tiffany Nat Cole became a stand-up singer, which Collins and Willard agree was Marie's idea.

segments.chapter: Fourteen years with Nat Cole and the recording sessions
segments.title: Copying Oscar Moore's solos when Nat's records were remade
segments.summary: Collins played the solos on remade Nat Cole records such as The Christmas Song, marked by a six-string chord at the end; live, Nat kept the solos.

segments.chapter: Fourteen years with Nat Cole and the recording sessions
segments.title: Nat Cole's policy of featuring only himself
segments.summary: Collins says no one could have changed Nat's mind about being the sole focus, and he kept practicing every day through those years.

segments.chapter: Fourteen years with Nat Cole and the recording sessions
segments.title: Classical guitar study, teaching Stanley Morgan, and his guitarist daughter
segments.summary: Collins studies classical guitar for technique, took lessons from Vince Macaluso, and mentions his daughter, a nun and classical guitarist.

segments.chapter: Fourteen years with Nat Cole and the recording sessions
segments.title: Recording with Nat Cole: redoing the trio hits note for note
segments.summary: He played on remakes like Mona Lisa and Paper Moon exactly as on the originals and did a few solos; musically the job stifled him.

segments.chapter: Fourteen years with Nat Cole and the recording sessions
segments.title: Bill Davis record with Duke Ellington
segments.summary: Before Nat, Collins recorded Bill Davis's date with Jo Jones and Duke Ellington, who invited himself; it began the Bill Davis trio.

segments.chapter: Fourteen years with Nat Cole and the recording sessions
segments.title: Illinois Jacquet sessions and Sir Charles Thompson's 'Robin's Nest' blowup
segments.summary: Collins played on Jacquet's records; when J. J. Johnson wrote a Robin's Nest follow-up, Sir Charles walked out and they recorded without piano.

segments.chapter: Fourteen years with Nat Cole and the recording sessions
segments.title: Dizzy Gillespie recordings and being everyone's first-call guitarist
segments.summary: He made about fifty records with Jacquet and nearly all of Dizzy's, and Willard says he was everybody's first choice in New York.

segments.chapter: Fourteen years with Nat Cole and the recording sessions
segments.title: Recording with Billie Holiday, Prez and Una Mae Carlisle
segments.summary: Collins names players he recorded with, including a late-night date with Billie and Lester Young and Victor sides with Una Mae Carlisle that were never promoted.

segments.chapter: Fourteen years with Nat Cole and the recording sessions
segments.title: Lester Young's rehearsal band and the Hammond booking dispute
segments.summary: Prez rehearsed a band at the Woodside; when he learned John Hammond would book him only as Billie Holiday's band, he dropped it.

segments.chapter: Fourteen years with Nat Cole and the recording sessions
segments.title: Betty Roche singing at rehearsals
segments.summary: Singer Betty Roche came by rehearsals daily; Collins compares her to Carmen McRae.

segments.chapter: Fourteen years with Nat Cole and the recording sessions
segments.title: Recording with Mildred Bailey in Chicago and New York
segments.summary: Bailey wanted Roy Eldridge, Teddy Wilson and Collins on her dates, recorded with the Three Deuces band in Chicago, and gave parties for musicians.

segments.chapter: Fourteen years with Nat Cole and the recording sessions
segments.title: Fletcher Henderson band personnel and what they taught him
segments.summary: Sandy Williams, Joe Keyes, Claude Jones and others taught him big band playing on Henderson's difficult charts and pulled jokes on him.

segments.chapter: Fourteen years with Nat Cole and the recording sessions
segments.title: Fletcher Henderson and Duke Ellington ignoring band grievances
segments.summary: Collins compares Henderson to Ellington, both indifferent to personal squabbles as long as the music was played, citing the 1951 Big Show.

segments.chapter: Fourteen years with Nat Cole and the recording sessions
segments.title: Coleman Hawkins at Cafe Society Downtown
segments.summary: After the army Collins worked with Hawkins, who drank all night and could play in any key, and recorded about thirty sides with him.

segments.chapter: Fourteen years with Nat Cole and the recording sessions
segments.title: Teaching and Irving Ashby in the army
segments.summary: Collins always taught guitarists and showed chords to Irving Ashby in the army at Fort Huachuca, who then joined Nat Cole.

segments.chapter: Fourteen years with Nat Cole and the recording sessions
segments.title: Ashby recording Collins's 'Bop Kick' under his own name
segments.summary: Ashby recorded Collins's melody Bop Kick with Nat and took credit; Collins did not hold it against him.

segments.chapter: Fourteen years with Nat Cole and the recording sessions
segments.title: Why Irving Ashby left Nat Cole: salary cuts
segments.summary: Ashby's drinking led Nat Cole, who never fired anyone, to cut his salary until he quit.

segments.chapter: Fourteen years with Nat Cole and the recording sessions
segments.title: Nat Cole building himself as a singer and hiding his piano
segments.summary: Collins understood Nat was building Nat Cole; on stage he got no solos, and Collins urged him to let the public see his piano playing.

segments.chapter: Fourteen years with Nat Cole and the recording sessions
segments.title: No guitar solos with Nat; the album After Midnight
segments.summary: Not being allowed to solo frustrated Collins and drove him to practice harder; he got several solos on the 1959 album After Midnight.

segments.chapter: Fourteen years with Nat Cole and the recording sessions
segments.title: Playing with Stuff Smith in Chicago
segments.summary: Collins haunted Stuff Smith's hotel group with Bernard Addison, Cozy Cole and John Brown and jammed with them in the dressing room.

segments.chapter: Fourteen years with Nat Cole and the recording sessions
segments.title: Black bands in Chicago hotels were the exception
segments.summary: Willard and Collins discuss how black bands rarely played Chicago hotels, such as the Hotel La Salle, and mention Eddie South behind a screen.

segments.chapter: Fourteen years with Nat Cole and the recording sessions
segments.title: Working with Frank Sinatra
segments.summary: Collins accompanied Sinatra on and off for about a year and praises his instinct as a musician.

segments.chapter: Fourteen years with Nat Cole and the recording sessions
segments.title: The Caesar's Palace incident and Sinatra's hands
segments.summary: Collins describes the morning of the alleged fight at Caesar's Palace and says the story that Sinatra hit someone was untrue since his tendonitis made it painful to hold anything.

segments.chapter: Fourteen years with Nat Cole and the recording sessions
segments.title: Sinatra's taste in musicians; Herbie Haymer
segments.summary: Willard recalls Sinatra's early West Coast bandmates; Collins calls Herbie Haymer a dear friend and says both Sinatra and Nat were thrilling to work with.

segments.chapter: Fourteen years with Nat Cole and the recording sessions
segments.title: Sammy Davis Jr. compared with Sinatra and Nat Cole
segments.summary: Collins says Davis was a mimic and dancer in an entourage show, while Sinatra and Cole were giants musically.

segments.chapter: Fourteen years with Nat Cole and the recording sessions
segments.title: Bobby Troup: the perfect job
segments.summary: Collins left Sinatra for Bobby Troup's trio for five years, doing all the playing, and got studio work around Hollywood.

segments.chapter: Fourteen years with Nat Cole and the recording sessions
segments.title: After Nat died: leaving Patti Page for Troup
segments.summary: After Cole died Collins quit Patti Page after catching himself signing Nat's name, and Troup gave him the job.

segments.chapter: Fourteen years with Nat Cole and the recording sessions
segments.title: Being kept in the dark on stage with Nat
segments.summary: Willard and Collins recall how only Nat was spotlighted and the sidemen could hardly be seen.

segments.chapter: Teaching, the 1951 Big Show and New York nights
segments.title: TV work and the Terry Gibbs band
segments.summary: Troup's job led to recordings and TV shows, including the Terry Gibbs band on Operation Entertainment, whose sax section became Supersax.

segments.chapter: Teaching, the 1951 Big Show and New York nights
segments.title: Teaching studio; Kenny Burrell as informal student
segments.summary: Students travel from Boston, Montana and San Francisco to study with Collins, who notes Burrell informally learned voicings from him.

segments.chapter: Teaching, the 1951 Big Show and New York nights
segments.title: How Collins teaches: playing tunes in many ways
segments.summary: He plays standards like How High the Moon many different ways so students absorb voicings by listening, and is compiling a book of tunes and original pieces.

segments.chapter: Teaching, the 1951 Big Show and New York nights
segments.title: Students sent by Barney Kessel and others; teaching as the future
segments.summary: Most of his students come by reference from guitarists such as Barney Kessel, and he expects eventually to concentrate on passing on what he knows.

segments.chapter: Teaching, the 1951 Big Show and New York nights
segments.title: Ella Fitzgerald album with Benny Carter and Georgie Auld
segments.summary: He recounts a recent Capitol album with Ella and Carter's all-star group, thirty tunes segued without a break, including a Hawaiian War Chant single.

segments.chapter: Teaching, the 1951 Big Show and New York nights
segments.title: Plans to record as a leader; Kenny Burrell and Dizzy offers
segments.summary: Collins has never recorded as a leader but intends to, with Jimmy Jones arranging; Burrell and Dizzy Gillespie want to record with him.

segments.chapter: Teaching, the 1951 Big Show and New York nights
segments.title: Ellington band on the 1951 Big Show; Paul Gonsalves as guitarist
segments.summary: Touring with Nat Cole and Duke Ellington's band, Collins notes Paul Gonsalves was a good guitarist and played Collins's guitar.

segments.chapter: Teaching, the 1951 Big Show and New York nights
segments.title: Louie Bellson and Jimmy Jones on the Big Show
segments.summary: Jimmy Jones accompanied Sarah Vaughan and haunted Duke and Strayhorn; only Nat could follow Louie Bellson's 'Skin Deep' closer on about eighty one-nighters.

segments.chapter: Teaching, the 1951 Big Show and New York nights
segments.title: Ray Nance jamming with Collins in the dressing room
segments.summary: Ray Nance played violin with Collins until Nat's turn, and Duke never mentioned his absence.

segments.chapter: Teaching, the 1951 Big Show and New York nights
segments.title: Strayhorn's lost arrangement of 'Unforgettable'
segments.summary: Strayhorn wrote a great arrangement of Unforgettable for Nat, but its baritone part went missing and could never be duplicated; Collins and Willard speculate who took it.

segments.chapter: Teaching, the 1951 Big Show and New York nights
segments.title: Watching Duke and Strayhorn play together by day
segments.summary: Collins and Jimmy Jones watched Ellington and Strayhorn play the auditorium piano as interchangeable partners.

segments.chapter: Teaching, the 1951 Big Show and New York nights
segments.title: Strayhorn's 'Strange Feeling' for his planned album
segments.summary: Collins plans to record the rarely played Strange Feeling and shows Jimmy Jones the Strayhorn record.

segments.chapter: Teaching, the 1951 Big Show and New York nights
segments.title: Life on the Big Show: Shorty Baker, Willie Smith's superstition, Cat Anderson
segments.summary: Players kept disappearing at hometown stops, and Willie Smith always waited to be last on the bandstand.

segments.chapter: Teaching, the 1951 Big Show and New York nights
segments.title: The 1952 Stan Kenton band
segments.summary: The following year he toured with Kenton's band, with Maynard Ferguson and Frank Rosolino.

segments.chapter: Teaching, the 1951 Big Show and New York nights
segments.title: All-night playing with Sal Salvador, Tal Farlow and Jimmy Raney
segments.summary: Four guitarists met nightly in New York for a year to play and talk, with Arv Garrison dropping in, while Collins stayed in town between Slam and Tadd Dameron.

segments.chapter: Teaching, the 1951 Big Show and New York nights
segments.title: New York versus Los Angeles; Panama Francis and Illinois Jacquet
segments.summary: Collins says New York musicians play from sheer desire, whereas Los Angeles is studio-oriented; he saw Panama Francis with Jacquet's band.

segments.chapter: Haiti, Artie Shaw and Los Angeles work
segments.title: Budd Johnson in Chicago
segments.summary: He met Johnson in Chicago in the early thirties and heard him in after-hours spots, ranking him with Lester Young and Ben Webster.

segments.chapter: Haiti, Artie Shaw and Los Angeles work
segments.title: Touring Haiti with Budd Johnson and Billy Taylor
segments.summary: Six weeks in Haiti with Johnson, Taylor, Lloyd Trotman, Charlie Smith and Kenny Dorham, living in a mountain town with voodoo drums at night.

segments.chapter: Haiti, Artie Shaw and Los Angeles work
segments.title: Budd Johnson in Quincy Jones's band in Europe
segments.summary: Years later Johnson toured Europe in Quincy Jones's band accompanying Nat Cole's show.

segments.chapter: Haiti, Artie Shaw and Los Angeles work
segments.title: Recording with Dinah Washington and Billy Taylor
segments.summary: In the forties Collins recorded with Dinah Washington and Paul Quinichette and often made small-group records with Billy Taylor.

segments.chapter: Haiti, Artie Shaw and Los Angeles work
segments.title: Billy Taylor and bassist Joe Benjamin; the Gramercy Five
segments.summary: Collins loves working with Billy Taylor, and Taylor, Joe Benjamin, Charlie Smith and Collins briefly formed Artie Shaw's Gramercy Five.

segments.chapter: Haiti, Artie Shaw and Los Angeles work
segments.title: Artie Shaw and the McCarthy blacklisting
segments.summary: Shaw lost bookings after being branded a communist and offered $10,000 to anyone who could prove it.

segments.chapter: Haiti, Artie Shaw and Los Angeles work
segments.title: Playing leftist rallies with Frankie Newton; Paul Robeson
segments.summary: Collins played three or four well-paid gigs a week at communist meetings with Frankie Newton and Flip Phillips, where Paul Robeson spoke.

segments.chapter: Haiti, Artie Shaw and Los Angeles work
segments.title: Artie Shaw studying semantics with Hayakawa
segments.summary: Shaw studied semantics with S. I. Hayakawa while the latter prepared Language in Action.

segments.chapter: Haiti, Artie Shaw and Los Angeles work
segments.title: Recording 'Autumn Leaves' with Shaw; talk sessions with the group
segments.summary: Collins played on one of the first recordings of Autumn Leaves with Shaw, and the group spent rehearsals talking, which Joe Benjamin loved.

segments.chapter: Haiti, Artie Shaw and Los Angeles work
segments.title: Last seeing Joe Benjamin at a Pennsylvania festival
segments.summary: At a late 1960s jazz festival with Troup, Collins unexpectedly met Joe Benjamin playing with Clark Terry and saw Earl Hines and Budd Johnson.

segments.chapter: Haiti, Artie Shaw and Los Angeles work
segments.title: Operation Entertainment with Terry Gibbs
segments.summary: The Chuck Barris show took bands to army camps for two seasons and was killed by sponsors' distaste for the Vietnam War.

segments.chapter: Haiti, Artie Shaw and Los Angeles work
segments.title: Substitutes at the China Trader and a trip to Mexico with Sammy Davis
segments.summary: Joe Pass, John Gray and Al Viola subbed for Collins at Troup's room while he did outside jobs.

segments.chapter: Haiti, Artie Shaw and Los Angeles work
segments.title: The Gramercy Five with Artie Shaw: musicians and the McCarthy pressure
segments.summary: Shaw's perfectionism and the quintet's quality; McCarthy-era pressure kept them from traveling, and afterwards Collins stayed with Billy Taylor's group.

segments.chapter: Haiti, Artie Shaw and Los Angeles work
segments.title: Recording with singers in California
segments.summary: He recorded with Carmen McRae, Julie London, Patti Page, Ramsey Lewis and Nancy Wilson.

segments.chapter: Haiti, Artie Shaw and Los Angeles work
segments.title: Private party gigs for the rich: Mexico with Nancy Wilson, Texas with Nat and Sarah
segments.summary: Collins describes one-night private jobs: nine models flown in for a Mexican host, and a Texas country club party for ten couples.

segments.chapter: Haiti, Artie Shaw and Los Angeles work
segments.title: Budd Johnson's timeless playing
segments.summary: Collins marvels that Johnson bridged eras and took charge as the old man in Quincy Jones's band.

segments.chapter: Haiti, Artie Shaw and Los Angeles work
segments.title: Benny Carter's all-saxophone date: Hawkins outplays Phil Woods on 'Midnight Sun'
segments.summary: On a 1964 Carter date with five saxophones, Hawkins took the solo and amazed Phil Woods by playing the tune every which way.

segments.chapter: Haiti, Artie Shaw and Los Angeles work
segments.title: Unpleasant Dixieland jobs in San Diego
segments.summary: Collins stopped taking pay gigs with Dixieland groups because the players were weak, not the style.

segments.chapter: Haiti, Artie Shaw and Los Angeles work
segments.title: Roy Eldridge dedicates 'Body and Soul' to him
segments.summary: At a recent New York gig, Eldridge announced that Collins had taught him Body and Soul in 1936.

segments.chapter: Haiti, Artie Shaw and Los Angeles work
segments.title: Victoria Bar and Grill: the tenor saxophone hangout near the Woodside
segments.summary: Hawkins, Dick Wilson, Joe Thomas and Prez gathered at the bar on 141st and Seventh, where players cashed recording checks and spent them.

segments.chapter: Looking back: rock, blues, childhood and guitar innovators
segments.title: Into the army; great players outlasting changes of style
segments.summary: Collins went in as soon as war was declared and stayed four years; he notes great players like Roy remain great.

segments.chapter: Looking back: rock, blues, childhood and guitar innovators
segments.title: How John Collins has changed: staying current with rock work
segments.summary: He likes innovation, plays with young musicians, and has recorded rock beats for Capitol and Motown with wah-wah and synthesizer.

segments.chapter: Looking back: rock, blues, childhood and guitar innovators
segments.title: Defending rock guitar and its blues roots
segments.summary: Collins says rock is hard to play, is an offshoot of the blues, and is a challenge he enjoys.

segments.chapter: Looking back: rock, blues, childhood and guitar innovators
segments.title: Records and minstrel shows in Montgomery
segments.summary: His mother's records of Armstrong, Bessie Smith and the classics, and the touring minstrel shows with good bands, were his music in a small town.

segments.chapter: Looking back: rock, blues, childhood and guitar innovators
segments.title: Blind blues guitarists and rock drawing on the blues
segments.summary: He remembers blind guitarists playing with bottle necks and says rock borrowed from Muddy Waters and other blues players.

segments.chapter: Looking back: rock, blues, childhood and guitar innovators
segments.title: Clarinet lessons he disliked
segments.summary: His mother chose clarinet and a Japanese teacher; he hated it at about ten and was drawn to strings.

segments.chapter: Looking back: rock, blues, childhood and guitar innovators
segments.title: Ukulele and banjo, then Selma and his mother's dance band
segments.summary: He was half-famous on ukulele, took up banjo to play in his mother's band, and they moved to Selma where she taught at Paine and led a dance band.

segments.chapter: Looking back: rock, blues, childhood and guitar innovators
segments.title: Correcting Chilton's Who's Who entry; Lee Collins and New Orleans trumpeters
segments.summary: Willard checks his mother's name (Gorham) and his entry, and he identifies New Orleans trumpeters like Lee Collins who moved to Chicago.

segments.chapter: Looking back: rock, blues, childhood and guitar innovators
segments.title: Studying with Frank Lanham in Chicago
segments.summary: Lanham taught him fundamentals and writing in the Electrum style instead of classical guitar, and introduced him to classical guitar history.

segments.chapter: Looking back: rock, blues, childhood and guitar innovators
segments.title: Roy Eldridge playing trumpet on his back
segments.summary: At the Three Deuces, Roy would get high and play lying down, apparently just as well.

segments.chapter: Looking back: rock, blues, childhood and guitar innovators
segments.title: Timeless stylists: Roy, Erroll Garner and Dizzy
segments.summary: Collins says individualists like Garner and Dizzy never changed and are as enjoyable now.

segments.chapter: Looking back: rock, blues, childhood and guitar innovators
segments.title: A concert with young musicians; Marshall Royal; Ellington's timelessness
segments.summary: After a concert with Jimmy Jones, Collins and Marshall Royal agree old timers must show the kids, and he cites Ellington's vigor.

segments.chapter: Looking back: rock, blues, childhood and guitar innovators
segments.title: Keeping learning: classical guitar, twelve-tone writing, the Schillinger system
segments.summary: Collins studies classics and twelve-tone scales so he knows what is happening, and says staying involved bridges the generational gap.

segments.chapter: Looking back: rock, blues, childhood and guitar innovators
segments.title: Armstrong, Roy, Dizzy and Charlie Shavers; 'My Man'
segments.summary: Collins traces trumpet innovation from Armstrong to Roy to Dizzy, and says he plays My Man because of Charlie Shavers's record.

segments.chapter: Looking back: rock, blues, childhood and guitar innovators
segments.title: Roy as world's greatest trumpeter; Dizzy jamming at the Savoy again
segments.summary: Collins repeats the Paul Whiteman poll story that took Eldridge's band to the Savoy opposite Erskine Hawkins, where only Dizzy would jam with Roy.

segments.chapter: Looking back: rock, blues, childhood and guitar innovators
segments.title: Dizzy Gillespie as the president of the trumpet
segments.summary: Collins says trumpeters all bow to Dizzy for his harmonic sense, and Dizzy's lineage of Louis, Roy, himself, Miles and Freddie Hubbard.

segments.chapter: Looking back: rock, blues, childhood and guitar innovators
segments.title: Young guitarist Pat Martino and the guitar boom
segments.summary: The guitar fad brings young players, and Collins is inspired by a Pat Martino record.

segments.chapter: Looking back: rock, blues, childhood and guitar innovators
segments.title: Dennis Sandole, teacher of Pat Martino and Coltrane
segments.summary: Collins visited Sandole in Philadelphia to study during Nat Cole layoffs, and Sandole mixed lessons with Jehovah's Witness preaching.

segments.chapter: Looking back: rock, blues, childhood and guitar innovators
segments.title: Joe Pass, Kenny Burrell, Lee Ritenour and other young guitarists
segments.summary: Collins is proud of a crop of young guitarists, including his student Lee Ritenour, whom he heard with Nelson Riddle.

segments.chapter: Looking back: rock, blues, childhood and guitar innovators
segments.title: Eddie Durham, Charlie Christian and Oscar Moore
segments.summary: He credits Durham as an early guitarist and Christian's exciting style, but says Oscar Moore thought like him harmonically before quitting playing.

segments.chapter: Looking back: rock, blues, childhood and guitar innovators
segments.title: Tal Farlow, Wes Montgomery, Joe Pass and other guitarists
segments.summary: Collins calls Wes Montgomery the most lyrical guitarist and lists Joe Pass, Pat Martino, Lee Ritenour and Howard Roberts.

segments.chapter: Looking back: rock, blues, childhood and guitar innovators
segments.title: Barney Kessel's wit: two stories
segments.summary: Collins tells Kessel's London bass player quip and his remark that Segovia is the king of one-nighters.

segments.chapter: Looking back: rock, blues, childhood and guitar innovators
segments.title: Sense of humor and being stranded after a club fire
segments.summary: Collins says jazz musicians need humor, recalling that on his first road trip with Roy in Pittsburgh the club burned with his guitar.

segments.chapter: Looking back: rock, blues, childhood and guitar innovators
segments.title: Crawford's Grill drummer Honey Boy; how Roy started on trumpet
segments.summary: In Pittsburgh he stayed to watch a fire-throwing drummer, and says Roy began as a drummer until his brother Joe bought him a trumpet.

segments.chapter: Chicago, the Woodside, the army and 52nd Street
segments.title: Joe Eldridge, Roy's brother
segments.summary: Joe was a fine writer and saxophonist who joined Roy's band when Scoops Carey left.

segments.chapter: Chicago, the Woodside, the army and 52nd Street
segments.title: Scoops Carey: saxophonist turned Chicago lawyer
segments.summary: Collins came up with Carey, who joined Tatum's sextet at the same time, played with Earl Hines, then became a lawyer and died of cancer.

segments.chapter: Chicago, the Woodside, the army and 52nd Street
segments.title: Meeting Jimmy Blanton and Floyd Smith in St. Louis and Pittsburgh
segments.summary: In 1936 with Roy he jammed all night with Blanton and Floyd Smith, and met Blanton again in Pittsburgh and New York.

segments.chapter: Chicago, the Woodside, the army and 52nd Street
segments.title: Blanton with Ellington and his illness
segments.summary: Blanton was featured with Duke, handsome and loved by Ben Webster, but visibly ill with TB.

segments.chapter: Chicago, the Woodside, the army and 52nd Street
segments.title: Midwest musicians: Budd Johnson, Jesse Price, Jesse Stone
segments.summary: Collins notes the Midwest produced strong swing reed men and drummers, including Lester Young, Buster Smith, Dick Wilson and Jesse Price.

segments.chapter: Chicago, the Woodside, the army and 52nd Street
segments.title: Touring with Roy: Gerald Wilson, the hurricane circuit, and returning to a sick mother
segments.summary: Roy's band picked up Gerald Wilson and Billy Bowen in Detroit, toured New England in a hurricane, and Collins went home because his mother was ill.

segments.chapter: Chicago, the Woodside, the army and 52nd Street
segments.title: Chicago, his mother's death, and the Arcadia Ballroom hostesses
segments.summary: After his mother died he rejoined Roy in New York at the Arcadia Ballroom opposite Les Brown, where hostesses made it a glorified taxi dance.

segments.chapter: Chicago, the Woodside, the army and 52nd Street
segments.title: Arcadia Ballroom band: Eli Robinson, Prince Robinson, Panama Francis
segments.summary: Collins names the strong players in the Arcadia band, unsure whether it was Roy's band.

segments.chapter: Chicago, the Woodside, the army and 52nd Street
segments.title: Kelly's Stables with Roy and singer Billy Daniels
segments.summary: Ken Corsey played piano at the Arcadia; at Kelly's Stables Billy Daniels arrived from the Black Cat, bringing his crowd.

segments.chapter: Chicago, the Woodside, the army and 52nd Street
segments.title: Jamming with Lester Young in Chicago; moving into the Woodside with Harold West
segments.summary: While in Chicago he and Harold West were Lester's jam rhythm section; in New York West put him up at the Woodside Hotel where Lester lived.

segments.chapter: Chicago, the Woodside, the army and 52nd Street
segments.title: Life at the Woodside: Harold West's cooking and rehearsing with Lester
segments.summary: Residents pooled money for groceries, and the group rehearsed with Prez and Shad Collins until Hammond's Billie Holiday plan broke it up.

segments.chapter: Chicago, the Woodside, the army and 52nd Street
segments.title: Lester Young's earthy wisdom and Chin Chow sayings
segments.summary: Prez was a profound man with earthy sayings, clipped Chin Chow's maxims daily, and expressed himself like no one else.

segments.chapter: Chicago, the Woodside, the army and 52nd Street
segments.title: Rehearsals without a piano; Clyde Hart joins; Prez's pride and shyness
segments.summary: They played a few jobs and recorded with Una Mae Carlisle; Prez quit jobs that did not suit him but was shy offstage.

segments.chapter: Chicago, the Woodside, the army and 52nd Street
segments.title: Lionel Hampton's band visits; Prez played chords by ear
segments.summary: Hampton's first band came to hear them rehearse, and Collins learned that Prez knew no chord names yet ran intricate patterns by ear.

segments.chapter: Chicago, the Woodside, the army and 52nd Street
segments.title: Army bands in South Carolina and Alabama
segments.summary: He served about four years, stuck in a weak South Carolina band that would not release him because he could read, before going to Oakland.

segments.chapter: Chicago, the Woodside, the army and 52nd Street
segments.title: Oakland: recording with Billie Holiday and Vernon Alley; Marshall Royal's navy band
segments.summary: Stationed in Oakland around 1945, he recorded with Billie Holiday at the Fairmont, and played with Vernon Alley and Marshall Royal's navy band.

segments.chapter: Chicago, the Woodside, the army and 52nd Street
segments.title: Hampton's band, Dinah Washington and T-Bone Walker in Oakland
segments.summary: Bands passing through Oakland included Hampton with Dinah Washington and Herbie Fields, and he nightly heard blues guitarist T-Bone Walker.

segments.chapter: Chicago, the Woodside, the army and 52nd Street
segments.title: Back in New York with Slam Stewart at the Three Deuces
segments.summary: After discharge he rejoined Slam Stewart with Billy Taylor and Harold West; the owner Sammy Kaye managed Slam, so they stayed at the club.

segments.chapter: Chicago, the Woodside, the army and 52nd Street
segments.title: Charlie Parker locking himself in the men's room
segments.summary: Opposite Collins's group, Parker played eight choruses then gave himself a fix in the men's room, and the door had to be broken down.

segments.chapter: Chicago, the Woodside, the army and 52nd Street
segments.title: 52nd Street stories: John Simmons, Leonard Feather and Ben Webster hitting Billie's dog
segments.summary: Collins and Willard swap stories of Simmons and Heywood's floating rhythm section, Simmons striking Feather, and Ben Webster knocking out Billie Holiday's dog's tooth.

segments.chapter: Chicago, the Woodside, the army and 52nd Street
segments.title: Rehearsing with Don Redman's band and playing hearts
segments.summary: Between jobs he rehearsed with Redman's band, where musicians played hearts and rehearsals started hours late.

segments.chapter: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
segments.title: Absent from the jazz books: Nat Hentoff's omission
segments.summary: Willard says no jazz reference books mention Collins; he complains Hentoff wrote about Scoops Carey yet left him out despite longer tenures with Tatum and Roy.

segments.chapter: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
segments.title: Willard's research; Esquire new star award and recordings with Jacquet and Dizzy
segments.summary: Willard found his name in only a few books; Collins cites his 1946 Esquire new star award and the many records with Jacquet, Gillespie and 52nd Street groups.

segments.chapter: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
segments.title: Going through his record labels: Sarah Vaughan, Billie Holiday, Eddie Davis
segments.summary: Collins pulls out records and reads personnels aloud, such as Sarah Vaughan with Jimmy Jones on Musicraft and Billie Holiday with Don Redman.

segments.chapter: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
segments.title: More labels: Julie London, Dameron's 'John's Delight', Billie Holiday and Teddy Wilson
segments.summary: He cites Vic Dickenson sessions, solos on Julie London dubbing, John's Delight and Focus with J. J. Johnson, and I Hear Music with Teddy Wilson.

segments.chapter: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
segments.title: More recordings with Mildred Bailey and Fletcher Henderson; 'like the shadow'
segments.summary: He lists Mildred Bailey dates, cannot recall his Henderson recordings, and says he is like a shadow though he spent fourteen years with Nat.

segments.chapter: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
segments.title: Maybe not colorful enough: no habits, no famous romances
segments.summary: Willard jokes he never wore a checkered hat, took drugs or got arrested, and Collins says he and Billie Holiday were once close.

segments.chapter: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
segments.title: Rudy Blesh's claim about Lester Young and Billie Holiday
segments.summary: Collins doubts Blesh's claim Prez ate at Billie's mother's place, saying he was eating with Harold West.

segments.chapter: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
segments.title: Complaining about omissions; After Midnight credits; Lady Sings the Blues
segments.summary: He jokes about shooting Hentoff and Feather, notes his After Midnight credit and film and stage work with Sinatra and Sammy Davis.

segments.chapter: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
segments.title: Known to musicians but not writers: a conspiracy?
segments.summary: Willard and Collins agree all musicians know him, yet critics ignore him; Willard has known his work for twenty years.

segments.chapter: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
segments.title: Tatum days: Murray McEachern, Ed Fant and the Goodman hire
segments.summary: At the Three Deuces trombonist Murray McEachern broke into the checkroom to play after hearing Ed Fant, and Goodman hired him; Collins also met Dorsey band members.

segments.chapter: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
segments.title: Mildred Bailey at the Blackhawk: recording with Roy's band
segments.summary: Collins jokes about chewing a guitar, then recalls Mildred Bailey recording in Chicago with Roy's band and Herbie Haymer while she worked at the Blackhawk.

segments.chapter: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
segments.title: The Three Deuces as a hangout; Gene Krupa
segments.summary: Because every touring musician came to the Three Deuces, Collins knew everyone on reaching New York, including Gene Krupa.

segments.chapter: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
segments.title: The missing critics
segments.summary: Willard notes no critics wrote in the Chicago days, and Collins again wonders why he is excluded.

segments.chapter: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
segments.title: Basie's first trip and New York as home; Mildred Bailey reunion
segments.summary: Collins met Basie in 1937, with guitarist Claude Williams, and musicians looked after each other; at the Golden Gate Ballroom Mildred Bailey rehired him for her dates.

segments.chapter: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
segments.title: Elbert Topps band and Dan Grissom
segments.summary: Collins confirms he first played with Elbert Topps, where his mother played and Dan Grissom was on saxophone.

segments.chapter: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
segments.title: Playing a black and tan after-hours club on 18th Street with Elbert Topps
segments.summary: As a young boy Collins played with his mother and Elbert Topps at an after-hours spot whose star was female impersonator Gloria Swanson.

segments.chapter: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
segments.title: Elbert Topps, drummer Bibbs, and his mother guarding him from the chorus girls
segments.summary: Topps was a fine trumpeter from Jackson, Mississippi, and Collins's mother protected him from the showgirls until the job closed.

segments.chapter: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
segments.title: What a black and tan club was; graft in prejudiced Chicago
segments.summary: Willard defines a black and tan as welcoming both races, and Collins says prejudiced Chicago was also graft-ridden, so almost anything could be bought off.

segments.chapter: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
segments.title: Bill Winston, the Topps drummer, now in Hawaii; Hubert Laws's band
segments.summary: Collins recalls another Topps drummer, Bill Winston, whom he met in Honolulu a year earlier while touring with Hubert Laws, and tries to remember other band members.

segments.chapter: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
segments.title: Meeting W. C. Handy in Montgomery
segments.summary: As a boy he met Handy at a concert in Montgomery, was struck by the production and the big brass section, and thinks it influenced him to be a musician.

segments.chapter: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
segments.title: Childhood records of Red Nichols and Louis Armstrong
segments.summary: He knew all the solos of Red Nichols's Five Pennies and Armstrong from records and could not choose between them.

segments.chapter: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
segments.title: Church music, Methodist and Baptist, and a daughter who is a nun
segments.summary: Collins played banjo in church, is a Catholic convert, recalls a moving a cappella spiritual by a Montgomery minister, and his nun daughter attended his concert.

segments.chapter: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
segments.title: Playing guitar and banjo in 'Lady Sings the Blues'
segments.summary: He played guitar and banjo in the Billie Holiday film and was consulted with Harry Edison, but the director wanted a love story, not her real story.

segments.chapter: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
segments.title: Music in the film, a scene in 'Blazing Saddles', and the instruments he plays
segments.summary: Other veterans did the Lady Sings the Blues music; Collins also played in a scene of Blazing Saddles with Basie and says he plays guitar, banjo, classical guitar and clarinet under protest.

segments.chapter: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
segments.title: Movie and TV studio work
segments.summary: He worked in films with Bobby Troup and on the Lucy Show, Bill Cosby, This Is Your Life and the Nancy Wilson Show.

segments.chapter: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
segments.title: Studio work versus playing jazz in clubs
segments.summary: Collins enjoys studio work, but Willard cites Shelly Manne and Ray Brown on losing jazz facility, and he says playing nightly with Troup was his outlet.

segments.chapter: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
segments.title: Art Tatum as a person: cards, photographic memory and beer
segments.summary: Tatum, about 90 percent blind, remembered every card in pinochle and Collins always partnered with him; they drank heavily together.

segments.chapter: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
segments.title: Tatum's reluctance to see Collins leave for Nat Cole
segments.summary: Tatum was under contract to Collins and unhappy that he left in St. Paul to join Nat at the Tiffany Club, but came to hear them nightly.

segments.chapter: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
segments.title: Tatum's last years in Los Angeles
segments.summary: Collins saw Tatum, weakened by illness, almost daily; Norman Granz recorded him, and Tatum showed Collins his new house in View Park.

segments.chapter: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
segments.title: Harlem after-hours with Tatum: Marlowe Morris and the piano players at Rubens
segments.summary: Between sets at Cafe Society, Tatum visited the Hollywood Club and Rubens, where Teddy Wilson and others played first and then Tatum wiped everyone out.

segments.chapter: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
segments.title: Scott Joplin's widow's after-hours apartment and Tatum's 'Danny Boy' joke
segments.summary: They went to Joplin's blind widow's flat where Tatum played, and he teased a traditionalist pianist with an outlandish chord in Danny Boy.

segments.chapter: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
segments.title: Tatum's love of sports and memory for batting champions
segments.summary: Collins describes track meets with Tatum and a Cleveland recording for a pilot's son while Tatum named a batting champion.

segments.chapter: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
segments.title: Recording with Tatum: 'Battery Bounce' and bad timing
segments.summary: Collins recorded with Tatum only once or twice, on unamplified guitar before the army, and missed a second chance when he left for Nat.

segments.chapter: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
segments.title: Tatum's reputation; Donald Lambert and Fats Waller
segments.summary: Tatum was known to all pianists, and Fats Waller took him to meet stride pianist Donald Lambert, who was crushed by Tatum's Tiger Rag.

segments.chapter: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
segments.title: Tatum waiting for everyone else to play before he sat down
segments.summary: Collins argues Tatum waited his turn not to cut anyone, because once he played no one else could.

segments.chapter: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
segments.title: Advice to young musicians: study the heritage
segments.summary: Collins urges young players to listen to earlier recordings, since what they do extends what was done before.

segments.chapter: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
segments.title: Putney Dandridge's bass lines at the Radio Inn
segments.summary: At the Radio Inn on 18th Street, he heard Dandridge's beautiful piano bass lines, which influenced him.

segments.chapter: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
segments.title: Lester Young's influence from Frankie Trumbauer
segments.summary: Collins notes Lester's debt to Trumbauer, which Lester confirmed, and traces the line to Getz and Al Cohn.

segments.chapter: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
segments.title: Guitar heritage: Eddie Durham, trombonists playing guitar, Christian's sources
segments.summary: The first black guitarist who influenced him was Eddie Durham, a trombonist, and he urges young guitarists to ask who influenced Christian.

segments.chapter: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
segments.title: Sidney Bechet and Benny Carter as giants
segments.summary: He heard Bechet with Noble Sissle's band, with Eddie Cole on bass, and praises Benny Carter's cultured style.

segments.chapter: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
segments.title: Rex Stewart and Freddie Hubbard
segments.summary: Hubbard's trumpet reminds Collins of Rex Stewart, another reason young players should go back and listen.

segments.chapter: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
segments.title: His grandmother Mary Jane Gorham: slavery, a plantation piano and a hostile film reaction
segments.summary: Collins's grandmother was sold as a girl, learned piano by watching her mistress's daughter, and a slave film left him angry as it matched her stories.

segments.chapter: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
segments.title: Old Ship AME and Mount Zion Baptist: choir practice and the blues in the church
segments.summary: His mother played at Old Ship Church and grandmother at Mount Zion, so he attended both choirs; he links blues to gospel expression.

segments.chapter: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
segments.title: Music among the slaves and secret learning
segments.summary: Collins says slaves held clandestine services and his grandmother practiced piano on the quiet because reading and writing were illegal.

segments.chapter: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
segments.title: His mother's career in Chicago and New York, sacrificed for her children
segments.summary: His mother made a name in Chicago and New York but returned to get her two children from their grandparents.

segments.chapter: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
segments.title: Kansas City, silent movie organ and drumming for Chauncey Downs
segments.summary: He lived in Kansas City, Kansas for a year while his mother played in theatres, and he once played drums with Chauncey Downs's band.

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: Paris 1947: French jazz fans booing bebop
segments.summary: On the 1947 trip with Slam Stewart, Hawkins and Howard McGhee, Hugues Panassie's seat block booed the bebop group at the Marini Theatre.

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: Booing in Paris again with Nat Cole, and Panassie's traditionalism
segments.summary: At the Salle Pleyel with Nat Cole the audience booed the opening French band, and Collins calls Panassie shortsighted for rejecting everything after Dixieland.

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: Kenny Clarke in Paris: first meeting and a borrowed pay
segments.summary: Collins met Clarke in Cincinnati with Roy and recorded with him in Paris for Nicole Barclay, where Clarke borrowed his pay.

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: Hawkins's welcome in Paris and 52nd Street Jazz with 'Epistrophy'
segments.summary: Parisians cheered Hawkins but booed McGhee; in 1946 Collins recorded 52nd Street Jazz with Fats Navarro, Sonny Stitt and Bud Powell.

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: Records with Illinois Jacquet and Dizzy Gillespie after the army
segments.summary: Collins lists personnels for Jacquet's Muttin' Leg and Dizzy's Oop Bop Sh'Bam dates, and says he was thrown straight back among the beboppers.

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: Lester Young's court-martial and his changed playing after the army
segments.summary: Willard cites Blesh on Prez's court-martial over a pill; Collins found him burned out and not the same Lester after discharge.

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: Why the army was wrong for Lester; Collins slipping away from training
segments.summary: Collins says regimentation and uncomprehending officers could destroy Prez, and describes dodging maneuvers until a master sergeant moved him into the band.

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: Refusing to unload boxcars in the Oakland port company
segments.summary: Placed in a port company in Oakland, Collins refused boxcar duty, was made to wash a hundred windows on Thanksgiving, and was transferred to a band camp.

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: Lester Young in Alabama: the guardhouse and the picture of his wife
segments.summary: Willard relates that Prez was jailed after a picture of his white wife was found; Collins knew only that he returned changed.

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: Meeting John Lewis through Kenny Clarke
segments.summary: After the war Collins heard John Lewis, whom Kenny Clarke had found in the army, and was impressed by the simplicity and depth of his playing.

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: Playing at Minton's and Monroe's Uptown House before and after Christian
segments.summary: Collins sat in at Minton's with Joe Guy, Monk, Nick Fenton and Scotty, amid pimps following musicians, and his first recording was with Mildred Bailey.

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: Billie Holiday at the Uptown House: Mildred Bailey, Jimmie Monroe and heavy drugs
segments.summary: Collins says Mildred Bailey admired Billie, who resented her; Jimmie Monroe allegedly started her on heroin, and Joe Guy followed, which Collins saw on the West Coast.

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: Why musicians used hard drugs
segments.summary: Collins says drugs had nothing to do with music and were an escape from social conditions, with young players imitating Charlie Parker.

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: Bird as a model; Collins on smoking pot
segments.summary: Collins heard Parker play worse when high; for himself pot was an escape from being poor, until he stopped when it hindered his playing.

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: Hawkins and Ray Nance as physical exceptions
segments.summary: Collins thinks some are chemically stronger, citing Hawkins drinking and snorting yet driving to Atlantic City, and saddened by Ray Nance not knowing him.

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: Billie Holiday crying at Ciro's
segments.summary: Billie Holiday came to Ciro's in Los Angeles around 1959 to pour out her regret about heroin, shortly before she died.

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: Hearing the Six Spirits of Rhythm and first smoking pot
segments.summary: Collins first heard the Six Spirits of Rhythm playing high at a pad and started smoking pot as an escape while his mother was ill and he waited tables.

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: Pot at the Three Deuces; the benzedrine Coca-Cola
segments.summary: At the Three Deuces everyone smoked on the bandstand and bought pot from the doorman Jumbo; at the Apollo, Billie handed him a Coke laced with benzedrine.

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: Tadd Dameron's addiction, arrest and death
segments.summary: Dameron lied about quitting, was busted by an undercover agent, then drank himself to death despite medical warnings.

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: Unpaid co-compositions with Dameron and an untitled tune Collins will record
segments.summary: Dameron took the money from tunes they wrote together such as John's Idea; Collins plans to record an unnamed one himself.

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: Ray Nance's Chicago band in 1932 and Lena Horne's arrival
segments.summary: Collins heard Nance's band at Dave's, played in Nance's big band, and once saw a beautiful Lena Horne step off Noble Sissle's bus.

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: Gangsters and Chicago clubs: Capone's Radio Inn
segments.summary: Collins says gangster-owned clubs gave musicians work and sometimes shooting, and the Radio Inn was rumored to be Capone's.

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: Ray Nance forms his own group; Scoops Carey joins Collins's mother's band
segments.summary: After high school Nance formed his own small group, while Grissom went to Lunceford and Scoops Carey replaced him with the mother's group.

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: How Art Tatum influenced his guitar playing
segments.summary: Sitting at the bend of the piano nightly broadened Collins's harmonic thinking, which showed after he left.

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: Regrets: leaving Tatum for Nat; declining Oscar Peterson
segments.summary: Collins says he should have stayed with Tatum and also should have gone with Oscar Peterson when Nat was in hospital, since Nat then stopped featuring him.

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: Fats Waller's sixteen-piece band jamming at the Three Deuces; Waller at the Howard Theatre
segments.summary: Waller brought his whole big band, with Al Casey, to jam in the small club, and later Collins saw him led on stage drunk at the Howard Theatre.

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: Ben Webster's character
segments.summary: Collins met Ben in Chicago in the early thirties, calls him warm and unique, and says he turned violent and could not play when drinking.

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: Ben Webster's drinking: Charlie Shavers and the Philadelphia hotel window
segments.summary: Ben once squared off at Shavers, and in Philadelphia he stuck his head through a hotel window, getting Collins's group thrown out.

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: Don Byas
segments.summary: Collins met Byas at the Three Deuces with Eddie Mallory's band, worked opposite him with Slam Stewart, and later in Holland, calling him intelligent and Hawkins-like.

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: Ben Webster's influences; Benny Carter born in New York
segments.summary: Collins thinks Ben sounded like Benny Carter on alto and notes Carter was a native New Yorker.

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: Chu Berry's driving style
segments.summary: Collins knew Chu Berry through Roy Eldridge, and contrasts his forceful chordal style with Ben's melodic playing.

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: Paul Whiteman's poll and Eldridge's Savoy booking
segments.summary: Willard asks whether Whiteman's Saturday Evening Post jazz poll mattered; Collins says it brought Roy work commercially, including the Savoy.

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: Dizzy and Ben Webster in Cab Calloway's band
segments.summary: Dizzy and Ben, both with Cab Calloway, played with Collins at the Grampion Hotel, and Calloway's band stretched out occasionally.

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: Lucky Millinder, bandleaders who sing and dance, and Ellington at seventy
segments.summary: Collins compares Millinder and Calloway's showmanship with Duke, who only danced and sang at seventy.

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: Henderson's band in Mississippi: the Rosedale sandwich shop
segments.summary: On the road in Mississippi, a white man in Rosedale told Collins to stand outside because the place was too small for white folks and 'niggers.'

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: Tupelo and Vicksburg: the singer Linda and the white promoter
segments.summary: Collins and the light-skinned vocalist were harassed by white men in Tupelo, and in Vicksburg the promoter terrorized her in her room.

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: Richfield, West Virginia: the restaurant fight
segments.summary: In a West Virginia restaurant the owner defended serving the band, white customers started a brawl, and the musicians fought their way out and were harassed at the dance.

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: Where Black bands stayed: rooming houses, and the Lafayette creole woman's house
segments.summary: Hotels were infested so bands used rooming houses; in Lafayette, Louisiana, a woman took him in but her white lover threw his bags onto the porch.

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: Frenchy the bus driver
segments.summary: Bus drivers knew where bands could stay; Frenchy drove Henderson's band, and Collins and Willard compare their experiences of him.

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: His godmother Jesse Knight
segments.summary: Collins lived with his godmother, a fair-skinned Montgomery pianist who worked as a governess and joined the post office in her sixties.

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: Mike Bryan and Tony D'Amico's apartment near Kelly's Stables
segments.summary: Two Memphis musicians, guitarist Mike Bryan and pianist Tony D'Amico, kept an apartment where musicians smoked between sets.

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: Recommending Mike Bryan to Goodman and receiving Christian's guitar
segments.summary: Collins recommended Bryan for Goodman, who got Christian's Gibson and amp, then gave them to Collins, causing nightly arguments with Roy.

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: Benny Carter recordings for Bob Freedman; Flip Phillips's photograph gift
segments.summary: Carter assembled top Los Angeles players to record songwriter Bob Freedman's tunes, and Flip Phillips gave Collins an old photo of himself with Lester Young.

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: The improvised score for 'Buck and the Preacher'
segments.summary: After Carter's score was rejected, guitarists and a mouth organ player improvised the soundtrack while watching the film.

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: Touring with Maria Muldaur and Benny Carter
segments.summary: Collins toured East Coast cities in Carter's band accompanying Muldaur, who sounded to him like a young Mildred Bailey.

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: Muldaur's idea for the Ellington-Kay Davis style 'Transblucency'
segments.summary: Carter told Collins the wordless voice-and-horn number was Muldaur's idea, and Willard says Kay Davis was surprised to be remembered.

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: More of Fletcher Henderson's 1940 personnel
segments.summary: Collins adds George Irish, Freddy Mitchell, Rudy Powell and Peanuts Holland to the band he remembers.

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: Working with Sinatra: no recordings, Al Viola, his musicians and politics
segments.summary: He never recorded with Sinatra but filled in for Al Viola, praised the musicians he carried and the stool duet, and disliked his later politics.

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: Why the all-night sessions with Farlow, Raney and Salvador were productive
segments.summary: Playing among themselves allowed repeats and the exchange of ideas without audience pressure.

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: The Benny Carter and Bob Freedman all-star band
segments.summary: Freedman, a retired manufacturer, hired Carter's dream band with Carmen McRae, Joe Williams and Ernestine Anderson singing.

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: Paul Robeson as a neighbor at Riverton
segments.summary: In later years Collins got to know Robeson in the Riverton apartments and says he sacrificed his career to make white America reckon with Black people.

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: Young musicians should study Black music history
segments.summary: Collins urges young players to study the history of Black music from Africa onward.

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: Musical rapport with Lester Young in Chicago
segments.summary: When Prez came to Chicago with Basie, he and Collins found each other and took over clubs to jam, including a 51st Street club with Israel Crosby's sisters.

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: The Woodside group: checkers with Clyde Hart and Prez after the war
segments.summary: In New York the Woodside group rehearsed daily with Betty Roche singing and Clyde Hart brought in; after the war Collins saw Prez was burned out.

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: Lee Young versus Lester Young
segments.summary: Collins says Lee Young was a good drummer with a businessman's sense of being in the right place, while Prez was all music.

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: Recent work with Neal Hefti and Billy May
segments.summary: Collins played with Neal Hefti's new band and recorded for Capitol with Billy May.

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: Detroit pianists who sounded like Art Tatum
segments.summary: Collins names Willie Hawkins of Detroit and Lanny Scott of Cleveland as pianists who sounded like Tatum, and mentions Al McKibbon and Kelly Martin.

segments.chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
segments.title: Closing of the Collins interview
segments.summary: Collins says that about wraps it up and Willard thanks him.

segments.chapter: Gillespie and Carter on John Collins
segments.title: Gillespie interview about Collins: header and Willard's question
segments.summary: Header for the March 29, 1975 interview with Dizzy Gillespie about John Collins and Willard's request to repeat his earlier statement.

segments.chapter: Gillespie and Carter on John Collins
segments.title: Gillespie on Collins the studious one and his advanced chords
segments.summary: Gillespie says Collins, before Charlie Christian, was always working out variations and chords, and was more advanced musically than the young Gillespie.

segments.chapter: Gillespie and Carter on John Collins
segments.title: Gillespie: Collins in Benny Carter's 1942 band and as a major guitar voice
segments.summary: They met around 1937 and worked together in Carter's 1942 band; before Christian, Collins was the guitar player.

segments.chapter: Gillespie and Carter on John Collins
segments.title: Gillespie on Collins's practicing and harp-like voicings
segments.summary: Gillespie says no book shows what Collins does, praises his constant practice, sophisticated progressions and a recent private harp-like demonstration.

segments.chapter: Gillespie and Carter on John Collins
segments.title: Gillespie: his own piano voicings and why Collins should make a solo album
segments.summary: Gillespie says he would play guitar like Collins, explains how he voices his arrangements, and wants Norman Granz to record Collins as a leader.

segments.chapter: Gillespie and Carter on John Collins
segments.title: Gillespie: Collins versus Charlie Christian
segments.summary: Gillespie says Christian was a blockbuster but not as deep as Collins, whose rhythm playing changes chords constantly, and he would rather play with him than anyone.

segments.chapter: Gillespie and Carter on John Collins
segments.title: Benny Carter interview about Collins: header
segments.summary: Header for the May 12, 1975 conversation between Willard and Benny Carter.

segments.chapter: Gillespie and Carter on John Collins
segments.title: Carter on recording with Collins: Definitions, Further Definitions and Thirty by Ella
segments.summary: Carter and Willard work out dates of their records together, including the five-saxophone album, and Carter will give her copies.

segments.chapter: Gillespie and Carter on John Collins
segments.title: Carter on Collins's underrated place and influence
segments.summary: Carter says Collins is not underrated by those who know him, agrees critics ignore him, and believes later guitarists were influenced by him.

segments.chapter: Gillespie and Carter on John Collins
segments.title: Goodbyes and archive plans for the transcripts
segments.summary: Willard explains the tapes will be kept at the Smithsonian with transcripts available on request, and they say goodbye.
